falsifiableTrigger: Combined accelerator output across NVIDIA, AMD, AWS, and Google fails to rise for 2 consecutive quarters, or packaging capacity per S10 stops expanding.
mechanism: NVIDIA, AMD, AWS, and Google are all ramping new accelerators to mass production at once, and expanding advanced-packaging capacity lets those ramps add up to more total supply in the second half of 2026.
rationale: The findings directly confirm the wave: NVIDIA Vera Rubin, AMD Helios, AWS Trainium 3, and Google chips are all moving into mass production at once, AMD's MI450 hits production in the second half of 2026, and expanding packaging capacity gives the ramps room, so total accelerator supply is set to rise into late 2026.
sensitivity: Whether advanced-packaging capacity keeps expanding fast enough to support all four ramps at once.

falsifiableTrigger: Any one of the named AMD mega-deals with Meta, OpenAI, or Oracle slips its deployment schedule by more than 1 quarter, or AMD Data Center revenue per D2 growth turns negative for 2 consecutive quarters.
mechanism: A few very large commitments from Meta, OpenAI, and Oracle drive most of AMD's accelerator growth, so the timing of those specific deals sets both its upside and its risk.
rationale: AMD's growth is visibly riding a few flagship commitments - up to 6 gigawatts with Meta, OpenAI as a core partner, Oracle, and a Rackspace deal - and AMD itself discloses reliance on a small number of customers, so its upside and downside both sit with a handful of partners.
sensitivity: Whether any single flagship customer delays or shrinks its committed deployment.

detail.falsifiableTrigger: Intel cancels or delays Crescent Island past its second-half 2026 sampling target, or no named cloud provider adopts an LPDDR-based inference GPU within 2 consecutive quarters.
detail.mechanism: By using standard LPDDR5X memory instead of high-bandwidth memory, an inference chip avoids the advanced-packaging and memory queues that limit other accelerators, so it can be built with capacity that is not fought over.
detail.sensitivity: Whether memory-based inference chips can deliver competitive performance without high-bandwidth memory.
detail.statement: Intel's Crescent Island inference GPU uses standard LPDDR5X memory instead of high-bandwidth memory to sidestep the advanced-packaging and memory bottleneck, opening an alternative supply route for inference chips.
detail.title: Memory-based inference chips route around the packaging bottleneck

falsifiableTrigger: Two consecutive quarters where NVIDIA datacenter revenue (D2) falls sequentially while stated lead times shorten.
mechanism: NVIDIA keeps setting datacenter revenue records and filling its order book quarters ahead while memory stays sold out, so buyers still cannot get all the accelerators they want.
rationale: NVIDIA set another datacenter revenue record at $75.2B up 92% YoY, guided the next quarter to $91.0B, cited ~$20B visibility with purchase orders from almost all major customers ahead of Vera Rubin, while HBM stays sold out and gates availability. A fresh doubt about AI-infrastructure ROI and a 67% capex jump appears but has not yet dented orders, so demand still outruns supply.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to hyperscaler capex holding up; a sustained cut to the $650B 2026 capex plan would close the demand-over-supply gap.

falsifiableTrigger: TSMC CoWoS supply-demand gap (leadTimes) widening back above 20% or HBM order books (S10) clearing before 2028.
mechanism: Packaging capacity is expanding faster than memory, so the ceiling on shippable accelerators now sits on the memory line rather than the packaging line.
rationale: ADJUSTED: High-bandwidth memory, not advanced packaging, is now the supply that caps how much merchant-GPU revenue vendors can book. Packaging is easing as the TSMC CoWoS gap narrows from about 20% to 10% by end 2026 and ASE and Hanmi add capacity, and NVIDIA's supply commitments run to $119.0B-$145B, while HBM3E/HBM4 stay sold out through 2027 with demand far above supply.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to HBM3E/HBM4 yield and the pace of the 16-Hi HBM4 ramp scheduled for Q4 2026.

falsifiableTrigger: AMD Instinct share of the AI accelerator market (market-share-pct) failing to rise above 7% through 2026, or AMD datacenter revenue (D2) growth stalling for two quarters.
mechanism: AMD's datacenter revenue keeps growing and it is signing multi-year Instinct deployments, but its accelerator share is still only a mid-single-digit slice next to NVIDIA.
rationale: AMD datacenter revenue reached $5.8B up 57% YoY with a Q2 guide near $11.2B, it signed a phased Rackspace Instinct deployment, MI450 moves to production in the second half of 2026, and Cantor lifted its target to $700. But AMD Instinct is still only about 5-7% of the AI accelerator market versus NVIDIA around 80%, so momentum continues without a share breakout.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to MI450/Helios production execution in the second half of 2026 and ROCm software maturity.

falsifiableTrigger: Custom-ASIC share of AI-chip shipments (market-share-pct) stalling below 27.8% or its 44.6% growth rate falling under merchant-GPU growth in 2026.
mechanism: Custom accelerators are growing far faster than merchant GPUs and taking a rising share of AI-chip shipments, which trims the growth that would otherwise flow to merchant GPUs.
rationale: Fresh figures put custom ASICs at 27.8% of AI-chip shipments growing 44.6% versus 16.1% for merchant GPUs, with Broadcom's $73B backlog and Anthropic's 2nm Samsung talks reinforcing the shift, which resolves the pending challenge toward the thesis. Supporting evidence spans only two publishers (tomshardware, techcrunch), so under anti-whipsaw the reversal from weakened is recorded but not applied, and the counter that GPUs remain ~60% of even AWS build-out while custom silicon stays captive keeps conviction bounded.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether custom silicon stays captive; if it remains internal-only with no external rental, merchant-GPU demand growth is little displaced in practice.

falsifiableTrigger: H100 rental $/GPU-hr (D6) or secondary resale (gpuSpotPrice) falling further quarter over quarter as Blackwell supply ramps.
mechanism: As Blackwell supply arrives, clouds are cutting older-generation H100 and H200 rental prices sharply, so rental levels are no longer holding up across the board.
note: pricing-power-persistence: applied: corroborated secondary reversal (3 distinct publishers; pending filing checkpoint)
rationale: Major clouds cut H100/H200/A100 rental prices up to 45% with H100 falling from peaks near $8/hr, and Blackwell availability is expected to push another 10-20% down on H100 secondary pricing. Newer parts like B300 at $7.39/GPU-hr still hold, but prior-generation levels are clearly no longer holding across the board.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to Blackwell ramp speed, which sets how fast prior-generation prices decay.

falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA China revenue (exportControlExposure) recovering above $9,000M in a single quarter, signaling the constraint no longer binds.
mechanism: Export rules erased NVIDIA's China Hopper sales and halved China revenue this cycle even as Washington shifts H200-class licensing from denial to case-by-case.
rationale: Export rules erased NVIDIA's China datacenter Hopper sales versus $4.6B a year earlier and halved China plus Hong Kong revenue to $4,550M, AMD took ~$440M in charges, and Taiwan is escalating smuggling probes. A shift of H200-class licensing from denial to case-by-case and Chinese buyers signaling purchases points the other way, so the constraint stays material but not more so.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to how many case-by-case H200 licenses actually convert to shipments versus staying at zero revenue.

falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA vendor-financed GPU commitments (rpoBacklog) climbing beyond the ~210,000 units across Firmus and Sharon AI in coming quarters.
mechanism: NVIDIA now guarantees revenue and buys back unused capacity for neoclouds that in turn buy its chips, so a growing slice of its demand is financed by NVIDIA itself.
rationale: NVIDIA launched a revenue-sharing and credit-support model, scaled CFO-approved vendor financing and rent-back guarantees across about 210,000 GPUs at Firmus and Sharon AI following CoreWeave $6.3B and Lambda $1.5B, and sold $25B of bonds, with multiple publishers flagging the circular-financing risk. This adds broad new corroboration that NVIDIA increasingly finances its own demand.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to neocloud creditworthiness; a single financed neocloud default would expose the circular loop.

falsifiableTrigger: Top-customer share of NVIDIA revenue (customerConcentration) falling below the prior 12/11/11 pattern, or the top three dropping under 21/17/16 percent.
mechanism: A handful of direct customers now buy over half of NVIDIA's revenue and their shares are rising, and vendor financing steers even more demand into a few neoclouds.
rationale: NVIDIA's Q1 filing shows three direct customers at 21%, 17% and 16% of revenue, and the annual filing shows one customer at 22% and another at 14%, up from a prior 12/11/11 pattern with the four largest more than half. Vendor financing further steers demand into a few neoclouds, so concentration is rising on fresh disclosure.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to any broadening of the buyer base beyond the current top four.

falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA losing its number-one datacenter Ethernet switch revenue rank (market-share-pct) within a year, or Spectrum-X attach to GPU sales falling quarter over quarter.
mechanism: NVIDIA became the revenue leader in datacenter Ethernet switching for the first time and bundles Spectrum-X and Quantum with Blackwell and GB300, tying networking to the GPU sale.
rationale: NVIDIA became the revenue leader in the global datacenter Ethernet switch market for the first time in Q1 2026, bundling Spectrum-X and Quantum with Blackwell and GB300. Taking the top switch rank while bundling is fresh, direct evidence that networking is deepening the full-system tie to the GPU sale.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to hyperscalers choosing merchant switching silicon over NVIDIA's bundled fabric.

falsifiableTrigger: A new NVIDIA generation failing to lower cost per token (flopsPerDollar), or AMD's per-dollar hardware edge translating into inference share gains within a year.
mechanism: Each NVIDIA generation cuts the cost per token, which makes more inference workloads worth running on its GPUs and enlarges the served market.
rationale: NVIDIA cites Grace Blackwell with NVLink delivering order-of-magnitude lower cost per token and says Vera Rubin extends the lead. AMD's MI300X shows a ~1.6x raw per-dollar edge in FP8, but that is hardware cost not system cost per token, so NVIDIA's each-generation cost-per-token drop still supports the demand pull.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to competitors matching cost-per-token at the system level, where AMD already shows a raw per-dollar edge.

falsifiableTrigger: Any of the 16 take-or-pay HBM contracts (rpoBacklog) being cancelled or deposits refunded within the 5-year term.
mechanism: Micron signed 16 non-cancelable five-year HBM contracts backed by more than $22B and about $18B of cash deposits, which pre-commits the memory that accelerators need and thus their future demand.
rationale: Micron signed 16 non-cancelable five-year take-or-pay HBM agreements backed by more than $22B with about $18B of cash deposits, and DRAM/NAND and HBM stay sold out through 2027 with order books into 2028. The scale of deposits is concrete new evidence that non-cancelable memory contracts pre-commit future accelerator demand.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to a demand air-pocket that would force buyers to forfeit deposits rather than take delivery.

falsifiableTrigger: Approved China licenses (exportControlExposure) lifting China revenue above the sub-50% cap, or the case-by-case window reverting to denial within two quarters.
mechanism: US policy now allows narrow, capped H200- and MI325-class licenses, so China reopens by exception rather than staying fully closed.
rationale: ADJUSTED: China datacenter compute is reopening to NVIDIA only through case-by-case H200- and MI325-class licenses capped under half of comparable US sales, with Chinese buyers now signaling first purchases. This cycle adds H200-class licensing shifted from denial to case-by-case and buyer interest from Alibaba, ByteDance and DeepSeek, broadening the earlier MI325-only picture, while China revenue sits at $4,550M and H200 licenses have booked no revenue yet.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether signaled Chinese H200 purchases actually clear licensing and generate revenue.

falsifiableTrigger: Additional frontier-scale models (S9) trained on non-NVIDIA accelerators within a year, or AMD ROCm design wins (releaseCadence) accelerating.
mechanism: A Chinese team trained a 1.6-trillion-parameter frontier model entirely on domestic non-NVIDIA chips, showing serious workloads can now run off the CUDA stack.
rationale: A Chinese team pretrained the 1.6-trillion-parameter LongCat-2.0 entirely on more than 50,000 domestic non-NVIDIA accelerators across 35T tokens, and AMD's MI350X is generally available on neocloud ROCm 7.0 with a raw per-dollar hardware edge. A frontier-scale model trained off the CUDA stack undercuts the claim that software difficulty keeps customers locked to NVIDIA.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to how portable mainstream training and inference software becomes across ROCm and custom stacks.

falsifiableTrigger: AI-server component cost inflation (S10) cooling below 1% per week, or DRAM/NAND pricing easing before 2027.
mechanism: AI-server rack component costs are climbing about 2-3% per week on memory and NVMe scarcity, directly raising the bill to build each server.
rationale: AI-server rack component costs are inflating about 2-3% per week, run 10-15% above baseline with up to a 40% weekly swing on memory and NVMe scarcity, and DRAM/NAND stay tight beyond 2027, direct support after last cycle's weakened read. This reverses direction on only two publishers (finance-biggo, www-investing), so under anti-whipsaw the move is recorded but not fully applied.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to when memory and NVMe supply loosens.

falsifiableTrigger: Any of Vera Rubin, MI450/Helios, Trainium 3 or Google TPU (releaseCadence) slipping mass production past 2H 2026, or HBM (leadTimes) throttling the combined ramp.
mechanism: NVIDIA, AMD, AWS and Google all reach mass production of next-generation accelerators in the second half of 2026, adding units, though shared memory scarcity caps how much total supply actually grows.
rationale: NVIDIA Vera Rubin, AMD Helios/MI450, AWS Trainium 3 and Google TPU are cited reaching mass production together in the second half of 2026, with Vera Rubin ramping Q3 2026 and MI450 in production in the second half. But HBM stays sold out through 2027 and gates GPU availability, so the simultaneous ramp is confirmed while the net supply expansion is capped.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to shared HBM and CoWoS supply, which all four vendors draw from.

falsifiableTrigger: AMD customer concentration (customerConcentration) easing to a broad base, or one large deal cancellation cutting datacenter revenue (D2) in a quarter.
mechanism: AMD says it depends on a small number of customers and its recent growth rides big commitments like the Rackspace 30 MW Instinct deployment, so a few contracts drive the trajectory.
rationale: AMD itself discloses it depends on a small number of customers and expects continued concentration, and its recent wins ride big commitments like the phased 30 MW Rackspace Instinct deployment, with analyst upside pinned to the MI450/Helios trajectory. AMD's own concentration disclosure is fresh, direct support that a few contracts drive its datacenter growth.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether MI450/Helios wins broaden beyond a handful of anchor customers.

falsifiableTrigger: Crescent Island (S9) missing its 2H 2026 sampling, or its LPDDR5X design still requiring the same advanced packaging capacity as HBM parts.
mechanism: Intel's Crescent Island inference GPU uses LPDDR5X instead of HBM, so it avoids the packaging and HBM contention that gates HBM-based accelerators.
rationale: Intel's Crescent Island datacenter inference GPU, shown at Computex 2026, uses LPDDR5X up to 480GB instead of HBM and is stated to avoid packaging and HBM contention, with sampling in the second half of 2026. This founding finding directly supports the thesis that memory-based inference chips sidestep the packaging bottleneck.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether LPDDR5X bandwidth is enough for real inference workloads at scale.

detail.falsifiableTrigger: TSMC wafer or CoWoS capacity (S10) running slack, or foundry prices flat to down over two quarters despite steady AI orders.
detail.mechanism: When every category of AI silicon competes for the same wafers and packaging, scarcity lets the foundry set higher prices.
detail.sensitivity: Most sensitive to how much CoWoS and advanced-node capacity comes online versus demand across all AI chip types.
detail.statement: AI demand spreading across GPUs, custom ASICs, networking and power chips fills TSMC's capacity across nodes and lets it raise prices.
detail.title: Broadening AI demand tightens TSMC capacity and pricing

detail.falsifiableTrigger: Hyperscaler AI capex (D2) growth reversing from the 67% jump toward $650B, or order cancellations appearing within two quarters.
detail.mechanism: If AI infrastructure fails to earn its keep, the buyers financing it will slow their spending and merchant-GPU orders will fall.
detail.sensitivity: Most sensitive to measured returns on deployed AI infrastructure over the next few quarters.
detail.statement: Hyperscalers' sharp jump in AI capital spending risks a pullback if returns disappoint, which would cut accelerator orders.
detail.title: Hyperscaler AI spending may outrun near-term returns

falsifiableTrigger: Two consecutive quarters where NVIDIA datacenter revenue (D2) falls sequentially while stated lead times shorten.
mechanism: Buyers order more compute than vendors can build because scarce memory and packaging cap how many accelerators ship each quarter.
rationale: NVIDIA posted record Data Center revenue of $75.2B (up 92% year over year, up 21% sequentially) and guided next quarter to $91.0B, with purchase orders in hand from nearly all major customers and roughly $20B of forward visibility, while memory supply stays sold out and packaging lead times run 52 to 78 weeks, so orders keep exceeding what vendors can ship.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether hyperscaler spending stays high and whether memory supply catches up to orders.

falsifiableTrigger: TSMC CoWoS supply-demand gap (leadTimes) widening back above 20% or HBM order books (S10) clearing before 2028.
mechanism: High-bandwidth memory stays sold out while packaging lines keep adding capacity, so memory now sets the ceiling on how many accelerators reach buyers.
rationale: Micron says memory shipment growth is capped by supply not demand, with high-bandwidth memory sold out through 2027 and order books reaching into 2028, while packaging capacity is expanding as the TSMC gap narrows from about 20% to 10% by end 2026 and ASE and Hanmi add lines, so memory remains the tighter cap even though packaging is still booked.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether memory makers can lift high-bandwidth output to meet 2027 to 2028 demand.

falsifiableTrigger: AMD Instinct share of the AI accelerator market (market-share-pct) failing to rise above 7% through 2026, or AMD datacenter revenue (D2) growth stalling for two quarters.
mechanism: Large multi-year commitments from Meta and Rackspace plus a maturing Instinct line give buyers a real second supplier they actually deploy.
rationale: AMD Data Center revenue rose 57% year over year to $5.8B with a next-quarter guide near $11.2B, and it landed large deployments including a Rackspace 30 MW build and a reported Meta commitment of up to 6 gigawatts of Instinct GPUs, with MI450 moving to production in the second half, so AMD is turning its roadmap into real deployments even though its share is still only about 5 to 7%.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether announced design wins convert into shipped share rather than staying paper commitments.

falsifiableTrigger: Custom-ASIC share of AI-chip shipments (market-share-pct) stalling below 27.8% or its 44.6% growth rate falling under merchant-GPU growth in 2026.
mechanism: Hyperscalers building their own chips grow those shipments far faster than merchant GPUs, so they take a rising share of new AI compute.
rationale: Custom AI chips are projected at 27.8% of the market in 2026 and growing 44.6% year over year versus 16.1% for merchant GPUs, Broadcom carries a $73B AI backlog targeting $100B by 2027, and Anthropic is exploring a custom chip, so in-house silicon is taking a rising slice of new compute even though these chips stay captive and GPUs still hold most of AWS builds.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether custom chips stay locked to their makers or become broadly rentable.

falsifiableTrigger: H100 rental $/GPU-hr (D6) or secondary resale (gpuSpotPrice) falling further quarter over quarter as Blackwell supply ramps.
mechanism: As new Blackwell and Rubin supply reaches the market, older H100 rental rates drift down toward commodity levels.
rationale: H100 cloud rentals now span roughly $1.49 to $6.98 per GPU-hour with most clustering at only $2 to $4, and new supply is arriving as Blackwell B300 reaches spot capacity and Vera Rubin ramps in the third quarter, so older-generation rental prices face downward pressure rather than holding firm.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to how fast new-generation supply floods the rental market.

falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA China revenue (exportControlExposure) recovering above $9,000M in a single quarter, signaling the constraint no longer binds.
mechanism: US license rules and tariffs block or tax the largest China datacenter GPU sales, cutting the market vendors can legally serve.
rationale: NVIDIA China revenue fell to $4,550M from $9,659M with no Hopper shipments last quarter and no revenue yet from H200 licenses, AMD took about $440M of related charges, and enforcement is intensifying via a smuggling probe, so export rules keep cutting the market vendors can legally serve despite a narrow case-by-case reopening.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether case-by-case licenses actually convert into shipped China revenue.

falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA vendor-financed GPU commitments (rpoBacklog) climbing beyond the ~210,000 units across Firmus and Sharon AI in coming quarters.
mechanism: NVIDIA lends money and guarantees to rent back idle GPUs so smaller clouds can buy its chips, which books demand that leans on NVIDIA's own credit.
rationale: NVIDIA has scaled a revenue-sharing and rent-back program backing about 210,000 GPUs across Firmus and Sharon AI, on top of CoreWeave and Lambda support deals, and raised $25B in bonds to fund it at scale, while CoreWeave's losses widened to $1.2B, so more reported demand now rests on NVIDIA-extended credit.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the financed clouds earn enough rental income to repay.

falsifiableTrigger: Top-customer share of NVIDIA revenue (customerConcentration) falling below the prior 12/11/11 pattern, or the top three dropping under 21/17/16 percent.
mechanism: A handful of large buyers make up over half of sales, so any one pulling back would dent revenue sharply.
rationale: NVIDIA now reports three direct customers at 21%, 17%, and 16% of total revenue, up from a 12/11/11 pattern a year earlier, with the four largest exceeding half of revenue, and its vendor-financing further concentrates demand in a few neoclouds, so reliance on a handful of buyers has clearly deepened.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the largest customers shift orders to their own in-house silicon.

falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA losing its number-one datacenter Ethernet switch revenue rank (market-share-pct) within a year, or Spectrum-X attach to GPU sales falling quarter over quarter.
mechanism: NVIDIA sells its switches together with its GPUs, so buying its accelerators pulls in its networking and raises the cost of switching away.
rationale: NVIDIA took the top revenue spot in the data-center Ethernet switch market for the first time in the first quarter of 2026 by pairing its Spectrum-X and Quantum networking with Blackwell and GB300, and its NVLink systems cut cost per token, so the bundled-system moat holds, though no finding shows networking outgrowing compute.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to open Ethernet alternatives eroding the bundled networking advantage.

falsifiableTrigger: A new NVIDIA generation failing to lower cost per token (flopsPerDollar), or AMD's per-dollar hardware edge translating into inference share gains within a year.
mechanism: Each new generation cuts the cost to serve a token, so more inference jobs become affordable to run on NVIDIA hardware.
rationale: NVIDIA states Grace Blackwell delivers an order-of-magnitude lower cost per token with Vera Rubin to extend the lead, and independent specs show a roughly 1.6x generational efficiency gain from H100 to B200, so each generation lowers the cost to serve inference, even as AMD keeps a paper cost-per-compute hardware edge that has not yet turned into inference share.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to AMD's hardware price edge converting into real inference deployments.

falsifiableTrigger: Any of the 16 take-or-pay HBM contracts (rpoBacklog) being cancelled or deposits refunded within the 5-year term.
mechanism: Buyers put billions in nonrefundable deposits behind multi-year memory contracts, so they are committed to take the chips those parts go into.
rationale: Micron has signed 16 non-cancelable five-year take-or-pay memory agreements backed by more than $22B in commitments including nearly $18B of cash deposits, with memory sold out through 2027 and next-generation parts already in development for NVIDIA, so a large slice of future accelerator demand is locked by real money.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the deposits are truly nonrefundable if demand softens.

falsifiableTrigger: Approved China licenses (exportControlExposure) lifting China revenue above the sub-50% cap, or the case-by-case window reverting to denial within two quarters.
mechanism: Regulators approve China sales one deal at a time under a hard ceiling, so access stays partial and slow.
rationale: Regulators still allow China sales only through case-by-case H200- and MI325-class licenses capped under half of comparable US sales and carrying a 25% tariff, buyers like Alibaba, ByteDance and DeepSeek are only signaling first purchases, and those licenses have booked no revenue against China revenue of $4,550M, so the reopening stays narrow and capped exactly as described.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether case-by-case approvals actually turn into shipped revenue.

falsifiableTrigger: Additional frontier-scale models (S9) trained on non-NVIDIA accelerators within a year, or AMD ROCm design wins (releaseCadence) accelerating.
mechanism: Rewriting AI software to run well on other chips is costly, so buyers with a choice tend to stay on NVIDIA even when rivals are cheaper.
rationale: Meituan trained its 1.6-trillion-parameter LongCat model entirely on more than 50,000 non-NVIDIA accelerators, AMD's MI350X is now generally available on clouds running mature ROCm software, and rivals hold a hardware price edge, so the software lock-in is leaking, though the training run was forced by China rules and still hit memory and ecosystem limits.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to how fast ROCm and other alternative software stacks mature.

falsifiableTrigger: AI-server memory bill-of-materials cost per S10 falls back toward baseline for 2 consecutive quarters, or DRAM output restrictions ease.
mechanism: Memory and storage chips are scarce and their prices climb weekly, so the parts bill for each AI server keeps rising.
rationale: NVIDIA AI-server rack component costs are climbing about 2 to 3% per week and sit 10 to 15% above baseline with swings up to 40% in a single week, driven by memory and storage scarcity that Micron expects to stay tight beyond 2027, so the parts bill for each AI server is clearly rising.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether memory and storage supply loosens.

falsifiableTrigger: Any of Vera Rubin, MI450/Helios, Trainium 3 or Google TPU (releaseCadence) slipping mass production past 2H 2026, or HBM (leadTimes) throttling the combined ramp.
mechanism: Four major vendors bring their newest accelerators to volume production in the same half-year, adding more total supply than any single ramp would.
rationale: Supply-chain reporting now shows NVIDIA Vera Rubin, AMD Helios, AWS Trainium 3 and Google TPU all moving into mass production at the same time, with Vera Rubin ramping in the third quarter and AMD MI450 shipping in the second half, so a combined supply wave in the back half of 2026 is well corroborated, subject to memory availability.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether memory supply gates the combined ramp.

falsifiableTrigger: AMD customer concentration (customerConcentration) easing to a broad base, or one large deal cancellation cutting datacenter revenue (D2) in a quarter.
mechanism: A few very large orders like Meta and Rackspace drive most of AMD's accelerator growth, so its results swing with a handful of partners.
rationale: AMD itself warns it depends on a small number of customers, and its accelerator growth now rests on a few very large commitments including a reported Meta plan of up to 6 gigawatts and a phased Rackspace deployment, so both its upside and downside sit with a handful of partners.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to any single mega-partner delaying or cancelling its order.

falsifiableTrigger: Crescent Island (S9) missing its 2H 2026 sampling, or its LPDDR5X design still requiring the same advanced packaging capacity as HBM parts.
mechanism: Using standard memory lets an inference chip skip the scarce advanced-packaging and high-bandwidth-memory steps that constrain other accelerators.
rationale: Intel detailed its Crescent Island inference GPU using standard LPDDR5X memory of up to 480GB instead of high-bandwidth memory to avoid advanced-packaging and memory contention, with a second-half 2026 sampling target, confirming an alternative supply path for inference chips.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether Crescent Island hits its sampling date and wins real inference workloads.

falsifiableTrigger: TSMC wafer or CoWoS capacity (S10) running slack, or foundry prices flat to down over two quarters despite steady AI orders.
mechanism: AI orders now come from many chip types at once, so they fill TSMC's lines across nodes and let it hold firm on price.
rationale: AI orders in 2026 are spreading beyond GPUs into custom chips, networking and power ICs, filling TSMC capacity across small and large nodes plus packaging and giving foundries pricing power, with packaging fully booked at 52 to 78 week lead times, a $73B ASIC backlog and NVIDIA's new networking lead all feeding the same lines.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the breadth of AI orders holds if any one segment slows.

falsifiableTrigger: Hyperscaler AI capex (D2) growth reversing from the 67% jump toward $650B, or order cancellations appearing within two quarters.
mechanism: If the sharp jump in AI spending fails to pay off, hyperscalers cut budgets and reduce chip orders.
rationale: Market sentiment turned to doubt in early July 2026 as analysts warned that hyperscalers' 67% jump in AI capex to $650B may be unsustainable, and a large buildout customer widened its net loss to $1.2B, so the risk of a spending pullback is live even while current orders stay strong.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to evidence over the next few quarters on whether AI spending earns a return.

detail.falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA non-GAAP gross margin (grossMargin) falling below 70% for two consecutive quarters.
detail.mechanism: Strong demand and software lock-in let NVIDIA charge premium prices, holding its gross margin near three-quarters while rivals earn far less per chip.
detail.sensitivity: Most sensitive to competitive pricing pressure from AMD and custom chips.
detail.statement: NVIDIA keeps its gross margin near three-quarters even while ramping new products, far above rivals, showing buyers still pay premium prices.
detail.title: NVIDIA holds a premium gross margin as it ramps new chips

detail.falsifiableTrigger: Top three CoWoS clients' share (S10) dropping below 70% within a year, or CoWoS lead times falling under 20 weeks.
detail.mechanism: Because three customers book most packaging slots, the packaging line's fortunes rise and fall with just those buyers' orders.
detail.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether NVIDIA and AMD orders hold through the ramp.
detail.statement: A few AI chip buyers control most of TSMC's advanced-packaging output, so any one of them cutting orders would leave capacity that is hard to refill.
detail.title: AI packaging supply is concentrated in a few buyers

falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA datacenter revenue (D2) falls sequentially for two consecutive quarters while stated lead times shorten.
mechanism: Memory and packaging suppliers cap how many chips NVIDIA can build, so buyers keep ordering more than it can ship.
rationale: NVIDIA posted record data-center revenue up sharply year over year and guided the next quarter far higher, while memory and packaging stay sold out and order flow keeps building, so demand still runs well ahead of what it can ship even as some analysts question spending.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether hyperscaler spending holds and to the pace of memory supply.

falsifiableTrigger: The advanced-packaging supply-demand gap (leadTimes) widens back above 20 percent, or high-bandwidth memory order books (S10) clear before 2028.
mechanism: Memory makers cannot expand high-bandwidth memory fast enough, so that memory sets the ceiling on how many accelerators vendors can ship.
rationale: Memory makers say high-bandwidth memory is sold out through 2027 with order books into 2028 and is the true ceiling on shipments, while packaging keeps easing as the TSMC gap narrows toward ten percent and new packaging capacity comes online, confirming memory rather than packaging as the binding limit.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to the pace at which memory makers add capacity.

falsifiableTrigger: AMD accelerator share of the AI market (market-share-pct) fails to rise above 7 percent through 2026, or its datacenter revenue (D2) growth stalls for two quarters.
mechanism: Large buyers are committing gigawatts of AMD accelerators, which turns AMD's roadmap into real deployed datacenter capacity.
rationale: AMD data-center revenue grew strongly, it raised its multi-year growth target, and OpenAI and Meta each committed gigawatts of AMD accelerators, turning the roadmap into real deployed share despite AMD still holding only a small slice today.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the gigawatt commitments convert to shipments and to AMD's packaging allocation.

falsifiableTrigger: Custom-ASIC share of AI-chip shipments (market-share-pct) stalls below 27.8 percent, or its 44.6 percent growth rate drops under merchant-GPU growth during 2026.
mechanism: Cloud giants build their own accelerators that grow faster than merchant GPUs, so a rising share of new AI compute skips buying NVIDIA and AMD chips.
rationale: Custom AI chips are projected to grow far faster than merchant GPUs and take a rising market share, one merchant ASIC vendor carries a very large backlog, and more buyers are pursuing in-house silicon, so custom chips increasingly absorb the growth that would have gone to merchant GPUs.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to the growth gap between custom chips and merchant GPUs.

falsifiableTrigger: H100 hourly rental prices (D6) or secondary resale prices (gpuSpotPrice) fall further quarter over quarter as Blackwell supply ramps.
mechanism: As new-generation supply ramps, buyers move off older chips, so rental prices for the older ones slide even while the newest stay firm.
rationale: Older-generation rental prices have slid further, with the same provider now listing roughly four dollars an hour against about seven a cycle ago, so price levels are not holding even though the newest chips stay firm and some spot pools remain tight.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to the pace of the Blackwell supply ramp and older-chip resale.

falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA China revenue (exportControlExposure) recovers above $9,000 million in a single quarter.
mechanism: License caps and tariffs shut NVIDIA and AMD out of most China datacenter sales, so a large block of potential demand cannot be served.
rationale: NVIDIA China revenue roughly halved year over year with no older-generation shipments and no revenue yet from newly licensed chips, and enforcement against chip diversion is intensifying, so the policy constraint is biting harder even as a narrow, capped reopening is discussed.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to US license policy and China approvals.

falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA vendor-financed GPU commitments (rpoBacklog) shrink below the roughly 210,000 units across Firmus and Sharon AI, or the revenue-share program is wound down within two quarters.
mechanism: NVIDIA lends to and guarantees payment for the clouds that buy its chips, so part of its reported demand rests on credit it extends itself.
rationale: NVIDIA scaled a revenue-share and backstop program covering roughly 210,000 GPUs across named cloud partners, funded in part by a large bond raise, so a growing slice of its reported demand rests on credit it extends itself, which several outlets flag as circular-financing risk.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to NVIDIA's willingness to extend credit and to the solvency of the financed clouds.

falsifiableTrigger: Top-customer share of NVIDIA revenue (customerConcentration) falls below the prior 12/11/11 pattern, or the top three drop under 21/17/16 percent.
mechanism: A handful of buyers make up more than half of NVIDIA's sales, so its revenue tilts further toward a few customers whose choices swing demand.
rationale: NVIDIA disclosed three direct customers at twenty-one, seventeen and sixteen percent of revenue and its four largest now exceed half of sales, up from a much flatter mix a year earlier, and vendor financing steers more demand toward a few clouds, so concentration is rising.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to hyperscaler order behavior and any shift to in-house silicon.

falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA loses its number-one datacenter Ethernet switch revenue rank (market-share-pct) within a year, or Spectrum-X attach to GPU sales falls quarter over quarter.
mechanism: NVIDIA sells its switches together with its GPUs, so buyers who want the full system stay with one supplier and face higher costs to switch away.
rationale: NVIDIA held its new top spot in data-center Ethernet switching by pairing its networking with its latest GPUs, supporting the bundled-system moat, but no finding compares networking growth against compute growth, so the claim stands where it did without new strengthening evidence.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to networking attach rates and competing switch offerings.

falsifiableTrigger: A new NVIDIA generation fails to lower cost per token (flopsPerDollar), or AMD's per-dollar hardware edge turns into inference share gains within a year.
mechanism: Each new NVIDIA generation lowers the price to run a given AI query, so more inference workloads become affordable and move onto its chips.
rationale: NVIDIA claims its newest system cuts inference cost per query by an order of magnitude and shows a clear generational efficiency gain, but a rival holds a per-dollar hardware edge and one measure has the prior generation cheaper on raw compute, so the pull-in mechanism holds without gaining ground.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to real-world cost per query versus vendor claims and to rival price-performance.

falsifiableTrigger: Any of the 16 take-or-pay memory contracts (rpoBacklog) is cancelled or its deposits refunded within the 5-year term.
mechanism: Buyers put billions in non-refundable deposits on multi-year memory contracts, so they are committed to build the accelerators that use that memory.
rationale: A memory maker disclosed sixteen non-cancelable five-year contracts backed by more than twenty billion dollars including roughly eighteen billion in deposits, and memory stays sold out through 2027, so a large share of future accelerator demand is now locked in by hard cash commitments.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to contract enforceability and buyer solvency.

falsifiableTrigger: Approved China licenses (exportControlExposure) lift China revenue above the sub-50 percent cap, or the case-by-case window reverts to denial within two quarters.
mechanism: US rules allow only reduced-capability chips into China under a volume cap, so sales can restart but cannot exceed a fraction of US demand.
rationale: US rules keep China access to case-by-case licenses capped under half of comparable US sales, buyer interest is now surfacing from a few Chinese firms, and licensed chips have booked no revenue yet with China revenue still depressed, matching the capped-reopening picture exactly.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to the pace of license approvals and Chinese buyer follow-through.

falsifiableTrigger: Additional frontier-scale models (S9) train on non-NVIDIA accelerators within a year, or AMD ROCm design wins (releaseCadence) accelerate.
mechanism: Moving existing AI code off NVIDIA's software stack is costly, so many customers stay even when competing chips are cheaper.
rationale: A frontier-scale Chinese model was trained entirely on non-NVIDIA hardware and AMD's software stack is now generally available with large new deployments, so the software lock-in the thesis relies on is eroding, though the moat still holds broadly since alternatives remain constrained and NVIDIA keeps most datacenter share.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to the maturity of alternative software stacks and to forced substitution under export controls.

falsifiableTrigger: AI-server memory bill-of-materials cost (S10) falls back toward baseline for 2 consecutive quarters, or DRAM output restrictions ease.
mechanism: Memory and storage prices are climbing fast, so each AI server costs more to build and buyers face bigger bills.
rationale: AI-server rack component costs are reported rising a few percent a week and sitting well above baseline on memory and storage scarcity, while memory stays sold out and a memory maker forecasts record margins, so build costs are climbing fast and pressuring buyer budgets.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to the memory and storage supply-demand balance.

falsifiableTrigger: Any of Vera Rubin, MI450/Helios, Trainium 3, or Google TPU (releaseCadence) slips mass production past the second half of 2026, or memory supply (leadTimes) throttles the combined ramp.
mechanism: Four major suppliers ramp new accelerators at the same time in the second half of 2026, so total available compute expands across vendors.
rationale: Reports confirm NVIDIA, AMD, AWS and Google accelerators all moving into mass production at the same time, with named ramp dates in the second half of 2026, so total accelerator supply is set to expand across vendors, subject only to memory throttling.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to memory and packaging supply throttling the combined ramp.

falsifiableTrigger: AMD customer concentration (customerConcentration) eases to a broad base, or one large deal cancellation cuts datacenter revenue (D2) in a quarter.
mechanism: A few very large customer commitments drive most of AMD's accelerator growth, so its upside and downside both ride on a handful of partners.
rationale: AMD's biggest new commitments come from just two customers each pledging gigawatts of chips, and AMD itself warns of continued customer concentration, so its accelerator growth and its downside both ride on a small set of partners.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the two anchor customers keep their commitments.

falsifiableTrigger: Crescent Island (S9) misses its second-half 2026 sampling, or its LPDDR5X design still needs the same advanced-packaging capacity as HBM parts.
mechanism: Intel's inference chip swaps scarce high-bandwidth memory for standard memory, so it can be built without competing for tight advanced-packaging supply.
rationale: Intel again detailed its inference chip using standard memory instead of high-bandwidth memory to avoid the packaging and memory crunch, with a second-half 2026 sampling target, so the alternative supply route stands as before with no new data to strengthen it.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to the sampling timeline and the chip's real packaging needs.

falsifiableTrigger: TSMC wafer or advanced-packaging capacity (S10) runs slack, or foundry prices stay flat to down over two quarters despite steady AI orders.
mechanism: AI orders now span many chip types, so TSMC's factories stay full and it can charge more across nodes.
rationale: Reports show AI demand spreading beyond GPUs into custom chips, networking and power parts, tightening TSMC across nodes and packaging and giving it pricing power, with packaging booked out more than a year and a large merchant ASIC backlog, confirming and reinforcing the tightening.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to the breadth of AI chip demand across nodes.

falsifiableTrigger: Hyperscaler AI capex (D2) growth reverses from the 67 percent jump toward $650 billion, or order cancellations appear within two quarters.
mechanism: Cloud giants spend far more on AI than they earn back so far, so weak returns could trigger a spending cut that reduces chip orders.
rationale: Analysts warn the sharp jump in hyperscaler capex may be unsustainable and one cloud's losses widened, keeping the pullback risk live, but a leading model provider's revenue is climbing fast and order flow is upbeat, so the risk stands without clearly increasing.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether AI revenue and returns keep pace with spending.

falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA non-GAAP gross margin (grossMargin) falls below 70 percent for two consecutive quarters.
mechanism: Buyers keep paying top prices for NVIDIA's newest chips, so its profit margin stays near three-quarters even during a product ramp.
rationale: NVIDIA held its non-GAAP gross margin at seventy-five percent with the same guidance while ramping new chips, far above a rival near the mid-fifties, so buyers are still paying premium prices, confirming the thesis on its first test.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to pricing power versus the cost of ramping new products and rising memory prices.

falsifiableTrigger: Top three advanced-packaging clients' share (S10) drops below 70 percent within a year, or advanced-packaging lead times fall under 20 weeks.
mechanism: A few buyers, led by NVIDIA, take the large majority of TSMC's advanced-packaging slots, so any one pulling back leaves capacity that is hard to refill.
rationale: The top three advanced-packaging clients take more than eighty-five percent of TSMC output with NVIDIA alone around sixty percent, and packaging stays fully booked, so a few buyers control most capacity and any one pulling back would leave slots hard to refill.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to how concentrated packaging demand stays among the top buyers.

detail.falsifiableTrigger: Weighted-average remaining life of supplier order books (rpoBacklog) shortens for two consecutive quarters, or the $21 billion and $73 billion multi-year commitments are cut.
detail.mechanism: Customers lock in multi-year compute purchases, so suppliers carry order books that stretch further into the future and steady near-term demand.
detail.sensitivity: Most sensitive to customer solvency and willingness to hold long-dated commitments.
detail.statement: Cloud and chip suppliers are signing longer-dated purchase commitments that push out the average life of their order books, so a growing share of AI compute demand is booked years in advance.
detail.title: Backlog duration lengthens as demand is booked years ahead

detail.falsifiableTrigger: Leading model-provider run-rate revenue (apiArr) falls or stalls for two consecutive quarters.
detail.mechanism: As model makers add paying customers their revenue climbs quickly, so they can fund large compute purchases from real income.
detail.sensitivity: Most sensitive to the durability of AI application revenue growth.
detail.statement: Leading AI model providers are growing revenue fast enough that their heavy compute spending rests on real and rising sales rather than hope.
detail.title: Model-provider revenue scales to underpin the buildout

falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA Data Center revenue (D2) falls quarter-over-quarter or CoWoS lead times drop below 12 weeks.
mechanism: Buyers place more orders and prepayments than the memory and packaging supply chain can convert into finished accelerators, so lead times stay long.
rationale: NVIDIA booked record Data Center revenue of $75.2B (+92% YoY) and guided Q2 to ~$91B, hyperscaler 2026 capex rose ~77%, and CoWoS plus HBM stayed sold out through 2027, so orders and prepaid commitments still exceed what NVIDIA can ship.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to HBM and CoWoS capacity additions catching up to order growth.

falsifiableTrigger: HBM4 contract prices (hbmSupplyCapex) fall quarter-over-quarter and HBM3E/HBM4 stop being sold out before 2027.
mechanism: HBM makers cannot grow shipments fast enough, so memory sets the cap on how many accelerators vendors can build and book.
rationale: Micron confirms HBM shipment growth is supply-capped with HBM3E/HBM4 sold out through 2027 and contract prices set to roughly double, the CoWoS gap narrows ~20%→10% while packaging stays fully booked, and NVIDIA's supply commitments stand at $119-145B, so memory remains the binding ceiling.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to HBM wafer capacity additions relative to CoWoS.

falsifiableTrigger: AMD Data Center revenue growth (D2) stalls below the prior quarter or its accelerator market-share-pct fails to rise above 7% within 4 quarters.
mechanism: AMD's Instinct wins at Meta, OpenAI, and Rackspace turn its roadmap into booked datacenter orders.
rationale: AMD Data Center revenue rose 57% to $5.8B with full-year growth guided near 114%, backed by Meta 6 GW, OpenAI, and Rackspace commitments, though its accelerator share is still only 5-7% versus NVIDIA's ~80%.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to AMD's CoWoS and HBM allocation versus NVIDIA.

falsifiableTrigger: Custom-ASIC share of AI accelerators (market-share-pct) stops rising above 28% or ASIC unit growth falls below merchant-GPU growth in a year.
mechanism: Broadcom-built TPUs and Trainium chips take a rising share of new AI compute, slowing merchant-GPU order growth.
rationale: Custom-ASIC shipments are projected to grow 44.6% YoY versus 16.1% for merchant GPUs toward 27.8% share, Broadcom's AI backlog hit $73B, and Anthropic and Meituan are moving to non-NVIDIA silicon, even as GPUs still hold ~60% of AWS builds.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether captive ASICs stay in-house or are sold as merchant parts.

falsifiableTrigger: gpuSpotPrice for H100 or H200 falls more than 15% quarter-over-quarter as new supply lands.
mechanism: New accelerator supply from several vendors adds rental capacity, which pushes spot GPU prices down.
rationale: Only a single low-confidence spot-price snapshot (H100 ~$27-40K, H200 ~$31-32K) speaks to price levels while a multi-vendor supply wave ramps in H2 2026, so there is not enough corroborated evidence to reverse the weakened stance.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to how fast H2 2026 supply reaches the rental market.

falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA China exportControlExposure revenue recovers above its year-earlier $9,659M level or H200 licenses book material revenue within 2 quarters.
mechanism: US license caps and China's own rules keep Blackwell and most Hopper out of China, cutting a large slice of addressable orders.
rationale: NVIDIA's China revenue fell to $4,550M from $9,659M with no Hopper shipments and Blackwell banned, H200 licenses booked no revenue, AMD took ~$440M in charges, and approved shipments stay trivial against demand for over 2 million H200 units.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to US and China license-policy changes.

falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA vendor-financed commitments (rpoBacklog) exceed the ~210,000-GPU level or a financed neocloud misses payment within 4 quarters.
mechanism: NVIDIA lends or takes revenue shares so neoclouds can buy its GPUs, so part of its demand traces back to its own financing.
rationale: NVIDIA expanded vendor financing and revenue-sharing to ~210,000 GPUs across Firmus and Sharon AI after CoreWeave ($6.3B) and Lambda ($1.5B), funded partly by $25B in new bonds, routing part of its demand through its own balance sheet.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to neocloud solvency and financing terms.

falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA's top-customer customerConcentration share rises above 22% next fiscal year or the top three exceed 60% in a quarter.
mechanism: A handful of hyperscalers and neoclouds now book over half of NVIDIA's data-center sales, so any one pulling back hits revenue hard.
rationale: NVIDIA's top three direct customers were 21%, 17%, and 16% of Q1 revenue and one customer reached 22% for FY2026 (up from 12%), with vendor-financed neoclouds adding to the concentration.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to hyperscaler capex allocation shifts.

falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA loses its data-center Ethernet switch revenue lead (market-share-pct) within 2 quarters.
mechanism: NVIDIA sells Spectrum-X Ethernet and Quantum InfiniBand alongside Blackwell systems, so buyers take the network with the GPUs.
rationale: NVIDIA became the data-center Ethernet switch revenue leader for the first time in Q1 2026, tied to Spectrum-X and Blackwell, which confirms the bundling claim; no finding compares networking versus compute growth, so the sharper claim stays unsupported.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to Arista and white-box Ethernet competition.

falsifiableTrigger: flopsPerDollar fails to improve with Vera Rubin or inference GPU demand growth stalls quarter-over-quarter.
mechanism: Each NVIDIA generation cuts the cost to serve a token, so more inference workloads become affordable to run on its GPUs.
rationale: NVIDIA reports Grace Blackwell delivering an order-of-magnitude lower cost per token with Vera Rubin to extend it, but this is a vendor claim with no independent evidence this cycle that lower cost is pulling in incremental inference.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to cheaper non-NVIDIA inference alternatives.

falsifiableTrigger: A signed HBM take-or-pay deal (rpoBacklog) is canceled or deposit-backed commitments fall below $22B within 4 quarters.
mechanism: Buyers post multi-year non-cancelable HBM deposits, so accelerator demand is contracted years before chips ship.
rationale: Micron signed 16 non-cancelable five-year take-or-pay HBM agreements backed by over $22B, and NVIDIA's supply commitments reached $119-145B, locking accelerator demand years ahead.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to buyer willingness to forfeit deposits if demand softens.

falsifiableTrigger: Approved China license value (exportControlExposure) converts to booked revenue above $4,550M in a quarter or the sub-50% cap is lifted.
mechanism: US grants only case-by-case H200 and MI325 licenses capped below half of US sales, so China compute reopens slowly while Blackwell stays banned.
rationale: The reopening stays capped: BIS grants only case-by-case H200/MI325 licenses under 50% of US sales, Alibaba, ByteDance, and DeepSeek are signaling first orders and ~10 firms cleared ~$10B in licenses, yet shipments remain trivial, Blackwell is banned, and revenue held at $4,550M.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to BIS license approvals converting into shipments.

falsifiableTrigger: A major buyer migrates production inference off CUDA (market-share-pct shift) or ROCm deployments exceed a set share within 4 quarters.
mechanism: AMD's ROCm 7.0 and Chinese domestic stacks now run large models without CUDA, so switching costs fall.
rationale: Meituan trained LongCat-2.0 entirely on 50,000+ domestic non-NVIDIA ASICs, AMD's MI350X shipped on ROCm 7.0, and AMD won Meta and OpenAI, all lowering the cost of leaving CUDA.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to ROCm and domestic-stack maturity.

falsifiableTrigger: AI-server memory and NVMe costs (hbmSupplyCapex) stop rising or fall quarter-over-quarter as supply catches up.
mechanism: HBM, DRAM, and NVMe shortages raise memory prices weekly, so each AI server costs more to build.
rationale: AI-server rack costs are rising 2-3% per week and 10-15% above baseline on memory and NVMe scarcity, with HBM4 prices set to roughly double into 2027 and DRAM and NAND tight beyond 2027.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to DRAM and NAND capacity additions.

falsifiableTrigger: Any of the four ramps (releaseCadence) slips past H2 2026 or 2H26 output misses plan.
mechanism: NVIDIA, AMD, AWS, and Google all move next-generation accelerators into mass production in the same half-year, so total supply steps up.
rationale: NVIDIA Vera Rubin, AMD Helios and MI450, AWS Trainium 3, and Google TPU all enter mass production in H2 2026, stepping up total accelerator supply.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to CoWoS and HBM allocation across the four ramps.

falsifiableTrigger: A single AMD design win (designWins) accounts for over 25% of DC GPU revenue or a named mega-deal is canceled within 4 quarters.
mechanism: A few outsized commitments from Meta and OpenAI drive most of AMD's data-center GPU growth, so losing one would dent the ramp.
rationale: AMD's growth concentrates in a few large commitments, with MI400 alone about $7.2B (~25% of DC sales), Meta 6 GW, OpenAI, and Rackspace as anchors, and AMD stating it depends on a small number of customers.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to concentration in Meta and OpenAI commitments.

falsifiableTrigger: Crescent Island sampling (releaseCadence) slips past 2H 2026 or LPDDR5X inference parts fail to reach volume within 4 quarters.
mechanism: Intel's Crescent Island uses LPDDR5X memory, so it needs no HBM or CoWoS advanced packaging.
rationale: Intel's Crescent Island inference GPU uses LPDDR5X instead of HBM and samples in 2H 2026, avoiding CoWoS and HBM; the single unchanged source supports the claim without adding weight.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether LPDDR5X inference performance is competitive.

falsifiableTrigger: TSMC gross margin (grossMargin) falls quarter-over-quarter or CoWoS drops below full booking in 2026.
mechanism: AI orders for GPUs, ASICs, networking, and power chips fill TSMC's leading-edge and CoWoS lines, so it raises prices and margins.
rationale: TSMC's Q2 gross margin rose to 67.7% (+9.1pp) with revenue up 36% and full-year guidance raised above 40%, CoWoS is sold out through 2027, and AI demand is broadening into ASICs, networking, and power chips.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to AI demand breadth holding across product types.

falsifiableTrigger: Hyperscaler 2026 capex guidance (hyperscalerCapexRevision) is cut quarter-over-quarter or a top hyperscaler announces an AI capex reduction.
mechanism: The four largest hyperscalers lifted 2026 capex to about $725B, so weak returns could trigger a spending cut.
rationale: Hyperscaler 2026 capex was revised up 77% to ~$725B (~75% AI) even as analysts warn the jump may be unsustainable, so the pullback risk stands, but no cut has occurred and the doubt is low-confidence.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to AI monetization pace versus capex.

falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA non-GAAP gross margin (grossMargin) falls below 70% in a quarter during the Rubin ramp.
mechanism: NVIDIA prices Blackwell and Rubin systems high enough that gross margin stays near 75% during the ramp.
rationale: NVIDIA held non-GAAP gross margin at 75.0% in Q1 and guided the same for Q2 while ramping Blackwell, keeping margin near three-quarters.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to memory-cost inflation and China mix.

falsifiableTrigger: Top-three CoWoS customerConcentration falls below 85% or a fourth buyer takes double-digit share within 4 quarters.
mechanism: NVIDIA takes about 60% and the top three buyers over 85% of TSMC's CoWoS output, so packaging supply sits in a few hands.
rationale: TSMC's top three CoWoS customers take over 85% of output, with NVIDIA ~60% and AMD ~11%, and AMD must split its slice between EPYC and MI400, so advanced packaging concentrates in a few buyers.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to new entrants winning CoWoS allocation.

falsifiableTrigger: Contracted backlog value (rpoBacklog) shrinks quarter-over-quarter or new commitments shorten below one year.
mechanism: Buyers sign multi-year deals like CoreWeave's Meta commitment through 2032 and five-year HBM take-or-pay, so order books stretch further out.
rationale: CoreWeave holds a $21B Meta commitment through 2032 and a $99.4B contracted backlog (up from $66.8B), Micron signed five-year take-or-pay deals, and Broadcom targets $100B by 2027, all pushing order books further out.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to buyer confidence in multi-year AI demand.

falsifiableTrigger: A leading model provider reports revenue (apiArr) growth stalling quarter-over-quarter while compute commitments keep growing.
mechanism: Model providers keep winning enterprise deployments like Claude on Azure, which points to rising paid usage behind the compute orders.
rationale: Model adoption keeps expanding, with Anthropic's Claude reaching general availability on Azure GB300 and OpenAI committing to AMD, but no finding this cycle reports model-provider revenue growth, so the claim holds only at low conviction.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether model revenue keeps pace with compute spending.

detail.falsifiableTrigger: A flagship Chinese model still needs smuggled NVIDIA GPUs (exportControlExposure) or domestic-ASIC clusters fail to scale past 50,000 chips within 4 quarters.
detail.mechanism: Chinese labs run full model training on domestic ASIC superpods, so every NVIDIA GPU they replace removes demand from the merchant market.
detail.sensitivity: Most sensitive to Chinese domestic ASIC yield and software maturity.
detail.statement: China's home-grown AI accelerators are starting to train large models without NVIDIA chips, cutting the country's need for imported GPUs.
detail.title: China Domestic Accelerators Displace Banned NVIDIA GPUs

detail.falsifiableTrigger: A major neocloud posts a net profit or its contracted backlog (rpoBacklog) falls quarter-over-quarter.
detail.mechanism: Neoclouds fund GPU purchases with debt and vendor credit while running net losses, so their orders depend on continued outside capital.
detail.sensitivity: Most sensitive to neocloud access to debt and equity funding.
detail.statement: Fast-growing neocloud GPU buyers such as CoreWeave are booking record revenue while their net losses widen.
detail.title: Neocloud GPU Buyers Grow Revenue but Deepen Losses

falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA Data Center revenue (D2) falls quarter over quarter, or CoWoS lead times drop below 12 weeks.
mechanism: Memory and packaging shortages cap how many GPUs NVIDIA can build while customers keep ordering more, so demand runs ahead of supply.
rationale: NVIDIA posted record Q1 FY2027 data center revenue up 92% year over year and 21% sequentially, guided the next quarter higher, and both memory and packaging remain sold out, so orders keep exceeding what it can ship.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to how fast memory and packaging capacity catch up to order volume.

falsifiableTrigger: HBM4 contract prices (hbmSupplyCapex) fall quarter over quarter and HBM3E/HBM4 stop being sold out before 2027.
mechanism: Memory makers cannot expand high-bandwidth memory fast enough, so it now sets the ceiling on how many accelerators vendors can build and sell.
rationale: Micron says high-bandwidth memory shipments are capped by supply with demand far above it through 2027-2028 and prices set to roughly double, while the packaging gap narrows toward 10% as ASE and Hanmi add capacity and NVIDIA's supply commitments run to $119 billion to $145 billion.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to how fast memory makers add high-bandwidth memory output relative to accelerator demand.

falsifiableTrigger: AMD Data Center revenue growth (D2) stalls below the prior quarter, or its accelerator market-share-pct fails to rise above 7% within 4 quarters.
mechanism: AMD is landing large multi-year orders from Meta, OpenAI and cloud providers that turn its Instinct roadmap into booked datacenter revenue.
rationale: AMD grew data center revenue 57% year over year, guided data center GPU revenue up about 114% for 2026, and locked in large commitments from Meta, OpenAI and Rackspace, though its accelerator share is still only about 5% to 7%.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether marquee wins convert into repeat volume orders rather than one-off deployments.

falsifiableTrigger: Custom-ASIC share of AI accelerators (market-share-pct) stops rising above 28%, or ASIC unit growth falls below merchant-GPU growth in a year.
mechanism: Hyperscalers ship their own inference chips and Broadcom-designed accelerators faster than merchant GPUs grow, taking a rising slice of new AI compute.
rationale: Custom ASIC shipments are projected to grow about 45% in 2026 versus 16% for merchant GPUs, reaching roughly 28% of the market, with Broadcom carrying a $73 billion AI backlog, even as GPUs still make up about 60% of AWS's build.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether captive chips stay in-house or absorb workloads that would otherwise buy merchant GPUs.

falsifiableTrigger: gpuSpotPrice for H100 or H200 falls more than 15% quarter over quarter as new supply lands.
mechanism: Tight memory and packaging supply keeps GPUs scarce, so rental and resale prices stay high even as new capacity arrives.
rationale: Secondary-market GPU prices stayed high and cloud rental rates held firm at $6.69 to $10.50 per GPU per hour, with no evidence of a sharp drop while supply stays tight.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to how much new capacity lands relative to demand over the next few quarters.

falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA China exportControlExposure revenue recovers above its year-earlier $9,659M level, or H200 licenses book material revenue within 2 quarters.
mechanism: US license rules, tariffs and enforcement keep NVIDIA and AMD largely out of China datacenter compute, cutting a large slice of addressable demand.
rationale: NVIDIA's China revenue fell to $4,550 million from $9,659 million a year earlier with no Hopper shipments booked, H200 licenses have generated no revenue, and AMD took about $440 million in China-related charges.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether case-by-case licenses convert into booked China shipments.

falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA vendor-financed commitments (rpoBacklog) exceed the ~210,000-GPU level, or a financed neocloud misses payment within 4 quarters.
mechanism: NVIDIA guarantees GPU purchases and rents back idle capacity for revenue share, so a growing part of its reported demand rests on credit it extends itself.
rationale: NVIDIA scaled a CFO-approved program that backstops roughly 210,000 GPUs at Firmus and Sharon AI for revenue share, funded by a $25 billion bond raise, and outside coverage flags the resulting circular-financing risk.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether financed neoclouds can pay from real end-customer revenue rather than more NVIDIA credit.

falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA's top-customer customerConcentration share rises above 22% next fiscal year, or the top three exceed 60% in a quarter.
mechanism: A handful of hyperscalers supply most of NVIDIA's revenue, so one of them slowing orders or moving to in-house chips would dent demand sharply.
rationale: NVIDIA's three largest direct customers were 21%, 17% and 16% of revenue this quarter, and its top customer reached 22% for the fiscal year, up from 12% a year earlier, with the four largest now over half of revenue.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the largest customers keep buying merchant GPUs or shift budget to their own silicon.

falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA loses its data-center Ethernet switch revenue lead (market-share-pct) within 2 quarters.
mechanism: NVIDIA sells its Spectrum-X and Quantum networking bundled with Blackwell systems, so buyers adopting its GPUs also take its switches, raising switching costs.
rationale: NVIDIA took the top revenue spot in data center Ethernet switching for the first time by bundling Spectrum-X and Quantum with Blackwell and GB300, and its NVLink systems lower cost per token, keeping the lead intact.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether open Ethernet rivals can unbundle networking from the GPU purchase.

falsifiableTrigger: flopsPerDollar fails to improve with Vera Rubin, or inference GPU demand growth stalls quarter over quarter.
mechanism: Each NVIDIA generation lowers the cost to run a given inference job, so more applications become affordable and shift onto its GPUs.
rationale: NVIDIA says Grace Blackwell with NVLink cut cost per token by roughly an order of magnitude with Vera Rubin to extend the lead, though AMD's MI300X still offers more raw compute per dollar on paper.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether rival chips or custom silicon undercut NVIDIA's cost per token.

falsifiableTrigger: A signed HBM take-or-pay deal (rpoBacklog) is canceled, or deposit-backed commitments fall below $22B within 4 quarters.
mechanism: Buyers prepay billions under non-cancelable multi-year memory contracts, so a large share of future accelerator output is committed and paid for in advance.
rationale: Micron signed 16 non-cancelable five-year take-or-pay memory contracts backed by more than $22 billion in cash and commitments including nearly $18 billion of deposits, while memory stays sold out through 2027.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether buyers honor deposits if AI demand cools.

falsifiableTrigger: Approved China license value (exportControlExposure) converts to booked revenue above $4,550M in a quarter, or the sub-50% cap is lifted.
mechanism: US rules allow only case-by-case H200-class licenses capped below half of comparable US sales, so China access reopens but stays limited even as buyers line up.
rationale: US policy still allows only case-by-case H200-class licenses capped below half of US sales, and while Alibaba, ByteDance and DeepSeek now signal interest, actual shipments stay trivial and China revenue sits at $4,550 million.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether approved licenses turn into actual shipments and whether the cap moves.

falsifiableTrigger: A major buyer migrates production inference off CUDA (market-share-pct shift), or ROCm deployments exceed a set share within 4 quarters.
mechanism: Rivals like AMD's ROCm and domestic chips now run real training and inference, chipping at the software advantage that kept buyers on NVIDIA.
rationale: AMD's MI350X is now generally available on clouds running ROCm, Meituan trained a 1.6-trillion-parameter model on over 50,000 non-NVIDIA chips, and Meta committed up to 6 gigawatts of AMD Instinct, all chipping at the software advantage.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to how portable production AI software becomes across ROCm and custom chips.

falsifiableTrigger: AI-server memory and NVMe costs (hbmSupplyCapex) stop rising or fall quarter over quarter as supply catches up.
mechanism: Memory and NVMe shortages drive weekly price jumps in AI-server parts, raising the cost to build each server and pressuring buyer budgets and margins.
rationale: AI-server rack component costs are rising about 2% to 3% per week and sit 10% to 15% above baseline, memory lead times stretched to 32 to 40-plus weeks with prices up about 90%, and memory contract prices are set to roughly double.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to when new memory capacity comes online relative to AI-server demand.

falsifiableTrigger: Any of the four ramps (releaseCadence) slips past H2 2026, or 2H26 output misses plan.
mechanism: NVIDIA, AMD, AWS and Google are all pushing next-generation accelerators into mass production at the same time, adding to total supply in late 2026.
rationale: NVIDIA Vera Rubin, AMD's MI400-series Helios, AWS Trainium 3 and Google TPU are all reported moving into mass production at once, with NVIDIA's ramp starting in Q3 2026 and AMD production in the second half, expanding supply into 2H26.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether shared memory and packaging supply can feed all four ramps at once.

falsifiableTrigger: A single AMD design win (designWins) accounts for over 25% of DC GPU revenue, or a named mega-deal is canceled within 4 quarters.
mechanism: A few very large commitments from Meta, OpenAI and cloud partners drive most of AMD's accelerator growth, so results hinge on keeping those specific deals.
rationale: A few large commitments drive AMD's accelerator growth, with Meta planning up to 6 gigawatts of Instinct, wins at OpenAI and Rackspace, and the MI400 line alone projected at about a quarter of data center sales, and AMD itself warns of customer concentration.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether any one flagship partner delays or cancels its deployment.

falsifiableTrigger: Crescent Island sampling (releaseCadence) slips past 2H 2026, or LPDDR5X inference parts fail to reach volume within 4 quarters.
mechanism: Intel's inference chip uses standard LPDDR5X memory instead of high-bandwidth memory, so it avoids the packaging and memory shortages that gate other accelerators.
rationale: Intel's Crescent Island inference GPU uses up to 480GB of standard LPDDR5X memory instead of high-bandwidth memory to avoid packaging and memory contention, and remains on track for second-half 2026 sampling.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether standard-memory parts deliver enough inference performance to attract buyers.

falsifiableTrigger: TSMC gross margin (grossMargin) falls quarter over quarter, or CoWoS drops below full booking in 2026.
mechanism: AI demand now spans GPUs, custom ASICs, networking and power chips, filling TSMC's capacity across nodes and letting it raise prices and margins.
rationale: TSMC lifted Q2 2026 gross margin to 67.7% and raised full-year revenue growth guidance above 40% as AI demand broadened into ASICs, networking and power chips, with CoWoS sold out through 2027 and capex raised to $60-64 billion.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether AI order breadth holds if any major buyer segment pulls back.

falsifiableTrigger: Hyperscaler 2026 capex guidance (hyperscalerCapexRevision) is cut quarter over quarter, or a top hyperscaler announces an AI capex reduction.
mechanism: Hyperscalers are raising AI capital spending far faster than proven returns, so disappointing payback could trigger a pullback that cuts accelerator orders.
rationale: Hyperscalers keep raising 2026 capex, with the four largest near $725 billion and Meta planning 7 gigawatts, but analysts began publicly questioning whether the roughly $650 billion AI spend can pay back, keeping the pullback risk live even though no cut has happened.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether AI revenue growth catches up to the capital being deployed.

falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA non-GAAP gross margin (grossMargin) falls below 70% in a quarter during the Rubin ramp.
mechanism: Buyers keep paying premium prices for NVIDIA GPUs, so it holds gross margin near 75% even while ramping new products, far above rivals.
rationale: NVIDIA held non-GAAP gross margin at 75.0% and guided the same for next quarter during its new-product ramp, far above AMD near 55% and TSMC at 67.7%, showing buyers still pay premium prices.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether competition or costs force NVIDIA to discount as new chips ramp.

falsifiableTrigger: Top-three CoWoS customerConcentration falls below 85%, or a fourth buyer takes double-digit share within 4 quarters.
mechanism: A few buyers led by NVIDIA book most of TSMC's advanced-packaging output, so any one cutting orders would leave capacity that is hard to refill.
rationale: The top three CoWoS customers account for over 85% of TSMC output, with NVIDIA near 60% and AMD about 11%, and AMD must even split its slice between CPUs and GPUs, confirming extreme buyer concentration.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether a new large packaging buyer emerges to diversify the base.

falsifiableTrigger: Contracted backlog value (rpoBacklog) shrinks quarter over quarter, or new commitments shorten below one year.
mechanism: Clouds and chip suppliers keep signing multi-year purchase deals, so a growing share of AI compute demand is locked in years before delivery.
rationale: CoreWeave's contracted backlog jumped to $99.4 billion from $66.8 billion including a Meta deal running to 2032, Micron signed five-year memory contracts, and Broadcom carries a $73 billion multi-year AI backlog, pushing order-book life out.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether long-dated commitments hold if AI demand softens.

falsifiableTrigger: A leading model provider reports revenue (apiArr) growth stalling quarter over quarter while compute commitments keep growing.
mechanism: Model providers fund their heavy compute spending out of their own sales, so the buildout is only durable if those sales keep rising.
rationale: Model providers kept committing to long-term compute and Anthropic reached production on Azure, but no finding shows their revenue actually rising, and analysts publicly doubted whether AI spending will pay back, so the claim that sales underpin the buildout is less supported this cycle.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether model providers disclose rising revenue rather than just larger compute commitments.

falsifiableTrigger: A flagship Chinese model still needs smuggled NVIDIA GPUs (exportControlExposure), or domestic-ASIC clusters fail to scale past 50,000 chips within 4 quarters.
mechanism: Chinese firms are training frontier-scale models on tens of thousands of domestic accelerators, so some Chinese AI compute no longer depends on imported NVIDIA GPUs.
rationale: Meituan pretrained a 1.6-trillion-parameter model on over 50,000 domestic non-NVIDIA chips, showing home-grown accelerators can train large models, though Chinese firms still ordered over 2 million H200 and viable in-house silicon at other labs is years out.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether domestic chips can match NVIDIA on memory and software at scale.

falsifiableTrigger: A major neocloud posts a net profit, or its contracted backlog (rpoBacklog) falls quarter over quarter.
mechanism: Neoclouds like CoreWeave book fast-rising revenue and huge backlogs but spend heavily on GPUs and debt, so their net losses widen even as sales grow.
rationale: CoreWeave grew revenue about 168% to $5.1 billion while its net loss widened to $1.2 billion, even as its backlog climbed toward $99.4 billion, matching the pattern of record revenue alongside deepening losses.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether rental revenue can cover GPU depreciation and financing costs.

detail.falsifiableTrigger: AI buildouts stop being sized in gigawatts, or planned power capacity growth stalls for 2 consecutive quarters.
