rationale: NVIDIA reported a 75.0% non-GAAP gross margin with the next quarter guided at the same level, confirmed by a second filing, while AMD ran at 55% and Intel at 40.4%, so the premium held through a product ramp and through rising memory costs.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to memory contract prices, which are forecast to roughly double into 2027 and sit inside the bill of materials.

falsifiableTrigger: Top-buyer customerConcentration in CoWoS output falls below 85% within a year.
mechanism: A handful of customers book nearly all the packaging line, so the supplier's utilisation depends on those same few order books staying full.
rationale: The top three advanced-packaging clients take over 85% of TSMC's output with NVIDIA at about 60% and AMD about 11%, and AMD must split its slice between server processors and accelerators, so a single buyer's pullback would leave capacity that is hard to refill.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether custom-chip and networking customers grow large enough to backfill a lost GPU booking.

falsifiableTrigger: Aggregate rpoBacklog duration shortens as new commitments turn shorter-dated over two quarters.
mechanism: Buyers who fear being short of compute sign longer contracts to hold a place in the queue, which pushes the average life of the order book further out.
rationale: Google Cloud's backlog rose more than $50 billion in the quarter to $514 billion with only just over half expected to convert within 24 months, Micron signed 16 five-year take-or-pay contracts, CoreWeave holds a $21 billion Meta commitment running to 2032, and its own backlog rose to $99.4 billion.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to supply loosening, since buyers stop pre-booking years ahead once parts are available on demand.

falsifiableTrigger: A leading model provider reports revenue (apiArr) growth stalling quarter over quarter while compute commitments keep growing.
mechanism: Model providers pay for compute out of paying customers rather than only out of investment money, so their orders rest on sales that already exist.
rationale: Anthropic's annual revenue run rate reached more than $30 billion as of April 2026, up from $1 billion in January 2025, and its compute chief ties further buying to meeting customer demand, with its models now in production on Blackwell Ultra systems in Azure; no other model provider's revenue appears in this cycle's findings.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to how much of that revenue is itself funded by chip vendors taking equity in the same model providers.

falsifiableTrigger: Chinese domestic accelerator designWins for frontier training stall over the next two quarters.
mechanism: With the best foreign parts blocked, Chinese buyers move spending to home-grown accelerators, which lifts those suppliers' sales even where performance still lags.
rationale: Beyond the earlier proof that a 1.6-trillion-parameter model was pretrained on more than 50,000 domestic accelerators over 35 trillion tokens, Chinese suppliers now show commercial volume, with Moore Threads guiding first-half revenue up 135-149% and Hygon up 56-70%, while Chinese firms still ordered over two million restricted NVIDIA parts against roughly 700,000 units of inventory.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether domestic supply can grow fast enough to cover the roughly two million units of unmet demand.

falsifiableTrigger: A neocloud's marginalBuyerFinancing debt load or net loss narrows for two consecutive quarters.
mechanism: Buying fleets on debt puts interest and depreciation on the books before the rental income arrives, so faster growth deepens the loss.
rationale: CoreWeave grew revenue about 168% from $1.9 billion to $5.1 billion while its net loss widened from $937 million to $1.2 billion, and it is roughly doubling capital spending to $31-35 billion against $14.9 billion last year with debt up 16.1% in one quarter.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to rental prices holding, since the loans were sized against today's hourly rates.

falsifiableTrigger: A top hyperscaler cuts its 2027 gigawatt power target below its 2026 level.
mechanism: A site can only run as many racks as it has electricity and grid gear for, so power decides deployment once chips are available.
rationale: Buyers now describe purchases in gigawatts rather than chips - Meta at 7 gigawatts in 2026 and roughly double in 2027, Anthropic at 2 gigawatts, OpenAI at 6, a Japanese site at 140 megawatts - while 40% of AI data centers are projected to be power-constrained by 2027 and power transformer lead times average 128 weeks.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to grid equipment lead times, which are far longer than chip lead times.

falsifiableTrigger: Broadcom-plus-Marvell market-share-pct of custom ASIC co-design falls below 90% within a year.
mechanism: Designing a competitive accelerator needs skills only a couple of firms sell, so the escape route from merchant GPUs runs through the same two suppliers.
rationale: Broadcom and Marvell together hold an estimated 95% of custom AI chip co-design and Broadcom alone carries a $73 billion order book, though an early-stage Anthropic approach to Samsung for a 2-nanometre custom chip hints at a third route that has not yet produced silicon.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether new entrants such as memory makers turn early talks into shipping designs.

falsifiableTrigger: Wistron odmMonthlyAiRevenue falls year-over-year for two consecutive months.
mechanism: Contract manufacturers only book revenue when finished servers leave the factory, so their monthly sales show real deliveries rather than orders.
rationale: Wistron posted record June revenue of NT$321.82 billion, up 53.9% year over year and 10.9% month over month on AI-server and networking shipments, opened a new 324,000-square-foot US plant for NVIDIA systems, and supply-chain players report the order boom spilling into the second half of 2026.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to memory and packaging shortfalls, which stall finished-system assembly even with orders in hand.

falsifiableTrigger: A neocloud's marginalBuyerFinancing debt-to-equity rises above 6:1 within two quarters.
mechanism: Fleets bought with borrowed money leave a small equity cushion, so a drop in rental income quickly threatens the loan payments.
rationale: CoreWeave has raised $18.81 billion of debt against $3.5 billion of equity, a 5.4-to-1 ratio, with total debt of $24.86 billion up 16.1% in a single quarter, while it plans $31-35 billion of 2026 capital spending.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to interest costs and to the vendor guarantees that currently backstop unused capacity.

falsifiableTrigger: Co-packaged optics adoption stalls below 5% of AI optical modules through 2027.
mechanism: Putting the optics inside the switch package saves power and cuts parts, which moves cluster wiring onto a different and faster-moving supply chain.
rationale: Co-packaged optics is forecast to go from about 0.5% of AI optical modules in 2026 to about 35% by 2030 with NVIDIA's photonics switches shipping this year, and Taiwanese packaging houses are newly competing for silicon photonics work as the technology enters commercial use.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to packaging yield, since the new optics compete for the same advanced-packaging capacity as accelerators.

falsifiableTrigger: A named US fab or packaging project slips its build milestone past 2027.
mechanism: Committed money and started construction move some fabrication and assembly outside Taiwan, which spreads where the same parts can be made.
rationale: NVIDIA plans up to $500 billion of US-made AI infrastructure with TSMC, Foxconn, Wistron, Corning and Amkor, Wistron opened a Texas plant, Micron committed $250 billion to US memory manufacturing with a New York groundbreaking, and TSMC added an incremental $100 billion US investment.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to construction and grid timelines, since announced money says nothing about when output starts.

falsifiableTrigger: Google Cloud or CoreWeave rpoBacklog fails to grow sequentially for two consecutive quarters.
mechanism: Providers cannot build capacity fast enough to serve signed contracts, so revenue measures their delivery rate while the backlog measures demand.
rationale: Google Cloud's backlog grew more than $50 billion in one quarter to $514 billion against $24.8 billion of quarterly revenue, and CoreWeave's backlog reached $99.4 billion against $5.1 billion of annual revenue, so committed contracts now dwarf what either can currently deliver.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to contract quality, since backlog counts commitments from customers who may themselves be vendor-funded.

falsifiableTrigger: A top hyperscaler returns to positive free cash flow while holding 2027 capex guidance for two consecutive quarters.
mechanism: Capital spending now exceeds the cash these businesses generate, so the shortfall is covered by issuing debt and shares.
rationale: Alphabet paid for its quarter's buildout with $49.6 billion of equity issuance and $20.3 billion of senior unsecured notes and reported its first-ever negative free cash flow of $5.9 billion, against combined 2026 plans of about $725 billion across the four largest buyers.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to credit and equity market appetite, which sets how long spending can outrun cash flow.

falsifiableTrigger: A new accelerator generation delivers less than a 1.5x perfPerWatt gain over its predecessor.
mechanism: More work per megawatt means a site with fixed electricity can serve more workloads without adding racks, which softens the power and packaging ceiling.
rationale: The newest rack-scale systems are stated to deliver about ten times the throughput per megawatt of the generation they replace and ten times lower inference cost per token, and the new photonics switching claims five times better power efficiency; an independent measure of the prior step showed a smaller 1.6x gain, still above the falsification line.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether vendor efficiency claims hold up in independent measurement, which has so far come in lower.

falsifiableTrigger: HBM leadTimes shorten and suppliers report unsold capacity for two consecutive quarters before end-2027.
mechanism: Each accelerator needs a fixed stack of memory, so the number of memory stacks a supplier can build sets the number of accelerators that can ship.
rationale: Micron says its stacked-memory shipment growth is capped by supply rather than demand and cannot yet see when the industry catches up, directly gating NVIDIA and AMD availability; Morgan Stanley sees no easing and flags worse shortages in 2027-2028, SK Hynix expects constraints through 2027, and suppliers met only 50-66% of demand.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to yield on the next memory generation, which uses three times the wafer capacity of standard parts.

falsifiableTrigger: Memory supplier gross margin falls for two consecutive quarters as contract prices flatten.
mechanism: Because memory is the scarcest part in the server, its makers set the price and take a bigger slice of what the finished system earns.
rationale: Micron's data-center segment earned $11.5 billion at an 87% gross margin, roughly double the prior quarter, while AMD ran at 55% and Intel at 40.4%, and next-generation memory contract prices are forecast to roughly double into 2027 with contracts already locked at high-teen to low-twenties percent increases.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to new memory capacity, since the margin rests entirely on scarcity rather than on a technology lead.

falsifiableTrigger: No new sovereign or enterprise cluster above 10,000 GPUs is announced for two consecutive quarters.
mechanism: Governments and large companies now buy clusters big enough to compete for the same scarce parts as the cloud giants, which widens the buyer base.
rationale: A Japanese national project with the trade ministry will deploy 27,500 Rubin GPUs across 140 megawatts, Firmus is building a 360-megawatt campus in Indonesia with up to 170,000 GPUs, Bristol Myers Squibb added a second enterprise system, Rackspace signed a phased 30-megawatt Instinct deployment, and AMD split its new line to serve sovereign buyers.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to national budgets and power availability at the chosen sites.

falsifiableTrigger: Intel data-center revenue growth falls below 10% year over year for two consecutive quarters.
mechanism: Better factory yields and outside foundry customers let Intel sell both its own server parts and manufacturing capacity, adding a third source of supply.
rationale: Intel's data-center and AI revenue reached $6.3 billion, up 59% year over year, foundry revenue reached $5.8 billion, up 31%, gross margin rose to 40.4% from 27.5%, next-quarter guidance beat expectations, and it added Fortinet as a named external foundry customer plus a EUR 5 billion Ireland expansion.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the first external foundry customers grow into volume, since the announced deals carry no disclosed size.

falsifiableTrigger: New vendor equity-for-compute deals in marginalBuyerFinancing stop appearing for two consecutive quarters.
mechanism: When the chip seller owns part of the buyer, some of the money paid for chips originally came from the seller, so reported demand partly reflects its own investment.
rationale: AMD committed a strategic equity investment of up to $5 billion in Anthropic alongside a 2-gigawatt compute deal, NVIDIA is buying $5 billion of Intel stock alongside a custom processor arrangement, and NVIDIA's revenue-share programme gives startups compute in exchange for a share of future sales.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the funded customers reach revenue that covers their compute bills on their own.

falsifiableTrigger: Standard DRAM S10 spot prices fall for two consecutive months as suppliers restore non-AI capacity.
mechanism: Memory makers move production lines to the higher-priced AI parts, which leaves less standard memory and lifts prices on everyday products.
rationale: AMD is raising graphics card bundle prices about 10-15% on tight memory supply with graphics memory spot prices roughly tripled since late 2025, older standard memory hit $81.20 above its prior peak and is up 17.5% in a month, and suppliers are cutting standard output to prioritise AI parts with all categories under allocation.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to when new fabrication capacity comes online, which suppliers place no earlier than late 2026.

falsifiableTrigger: No new multi-year accelerator-to-memory supply partnership is announced for two consecutive quarters through 2027.
mechanism: With memory the scarcest input, accelerator makers contract straight with the memory suppliers to reserve output rather than compete for it later on the open market.
rationale: NVIDIA entered a long-term partnership with SK hynix to secure next-generation memory and jointly develop it, part of a $500-billion-plus SK Group arrangement covering AI factory construction and memory supply, all three memory makers began full-scale development of 16-high next-generation stacks for NVIDIA, and NVIDIA's supply commitments including prepayments rose to $145 billion.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to memory supply loosening, which would remove the reason to lock output years ahead.

falsifiableTrigger: The leading supplier's HBM market-share-pct falls below 50% within four quarters as rivals ship volume.
mechanism: One supplier makes most of the memory that accelerators need and its output is pre-sold to the largest buyers, so smaller buyers cannot get parts at any price.
rationale: SK Hynix holds 56.4% of the stacked-memory market, NVIDIA has now signed a long-term supply and joint development partnership with it, and Microsoft, Google and Meta have used cash reserves to lock long-term contracts, though Samsung is adding 50% capacity and Micron is investing heavily, which could dilute that lead.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to rival yields on the next memory generation, since qualification is what actually shifts share.

falsifiableTrigger: No new diversion prosecution or whitelist reduction is reported for two consecutive quarters.
mechanism: Prosecutions and a shorter approved-buyer list raise the personal and commercial cost of reselling restricted parts, which shuts the informal channels.
rationale: Taiwanese prosecutors expanded a criminal smuggling probe with raids on Super Micro's Taiwan office and affiliates and detained employees, tied to US charges over some $2.5 billion of servers shipped without a licence, and NVIDIA more than halved the number of authorised Asian buyers under a new compliance whitelist.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to the size of the price gap between licensed and unlicensed supply, which sets how much smuggling pays.

detail.falsifiableTrigger: CoWoS lead times stay above 52 weeks through the end of 2027 while the supply gap fails to narrow below 15%.
detail.mechanism: Packaging capacity can be added by building more lines and hiring outside assembly partners, while memory needs new fabs and better yields, so the two constraints loosen on different clocks.
detail.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether outside assembly partners can qualify at the same quality as the lead supplier.
detail.statement: The advanced-packaging shortage is set to narrow over the next year as capacity expands and outside assembly partners join in, leaving memory as the tighter of the two limits on accelerator output.
detail.title: Packaging tightness starts to ease while memory does not

detail.falsifiableTrigger: NAND contract prices for server drives fall for two consecutive quarters while Rubin deployments keep growing.
detail.mechanism: A new hardware tier that needs hundreds of drives per unit adds demand for flash faster than makers can add lines, so its price and lead time climb like memory's did.
detail.sensitivity: Most sensitive to how quickly Rubin-generation racks actually deploy, since the demand step depends on that ramp.
detail.statement: The newest accelerator generation adds a large storage tier that is pulling flash demand up sharply and is already showing up as rising server costs.
detail.title: Storage becomes the next scarce part in the AI rack

detail.falsifiableTrigger: Public list rates for the newest rack-scale systems appear on major provider pricing pages within two quarters.
detail.mechanism: When the newest hardware is scarce, providers hold back list prices and negotiate each contract, which keeps the highest prices out of public view.
detail.sensitivity: Most sensitive to supply loosening, since providers publish rates again once they need to fill idle capacity.
detail.statement: Cloud providers publish rates for last-generation accelerators but quote their newest systems only through sales, so listed prices no longer show what the leading edge costs.
detail.title: The newest systems leave the public price list

falsifiableTrigger: B200 rpoBacklog falls below 2 million units for two consecutive quarters.
mechanism: Buyers keep committing to more accelerators than NVIDIA can build, so the company sells everything it makes and still carries a large unfilled order book.
rationale: NVIDIA posted record quarterly data-center revenue of $75.2 billion, up 92% from a year earlier, and guided the next quarter to $91.0 billion; its newest rack systems entered production ramp with major cloud and enterprise buyers already committed, an order book of about 3.6 million units for the prior generation is still outstanding, and the company is negotiating more than $750 billion of further infrastructure agreements. Orders keep arriving faster than parts can be built.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to a cut in cloud capital-spending plans, which would shrink the forward order book before shipments ever slow.

falsifiableTrigger: HBM leadTimes ease to available-on-demand and CoWoS lead times fall below 26 weeks before the end of 2027.
mechanism: Every accelerator needs both a stack of high-speed memory and a slot on an advanced packaging line, so whichever of the two is scarcer sets the shipment ceiling.
rationale: TSMC's advanced packaging is sold out with lead times of 52 to 78 weeks and bookings into 2027 even as capacity climbs toward 125,000 to 130,000 wafers a month, and TSMC says the gap between demand and supply stays very big through 2029-2030; stacked memory is sold out through 2026 with much of 2027 pre-booked, and Micron says its shipment growth is capped by supply rather than demand. Both limits still bind at once.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to how fast new packaging lines and memory fabs come online relative to each new accelerator generation's memory content.

falsifiableTrigger: AMD accelerator market-share-pct fails to rise above 7% through 2027.
mechanism: Large buyers want a second supplier for bargaining power and delivery certainty, so AMD wins volume commitments once its rack-scale product and software are good enough to run production work.
rationale: AMD put its Helios rack system into production with named commitments from Anthropic at up to 2 gigawatts, OpenAI at 6 gigawatts, Meta at up to 6 gigawatts, Microsoft, Oracle and Rackspace, and its data-center revenue rose 57% to $5.78 billion with analysts modelling roughly $15 billion of data-center GPU sales this year. Share is still only about 5% to 7%, and one report says the rack-scale volume ramp only reaches production tokens in the second quarter of 2027, so the conversion is real but not yet visible in share.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the Helios racks ship on schedule and whether AMD can get enough packaging and memory allocation to fill the commitments.

falsifiableTrigger: ASIC market-share-pct growth falls back below GPU growth for two consecutive quarters.
mechanism: Cloud operators build their own inference chips to cut the price they pay per unit of work, so each in-house part they deploy is a merchant GPU they do not buy.
rationale: Custom chips are forecast to grow 44.6% this year against 16.1% for merchant GPUs, reaching about 27.8% of AI servers, hyperscaler in-house silicon spending is projected above $25 billion, Meta's four new in-house accelerators enter production in September aimed at cutting GPU purchases, and NVIDIA's accelerator share is projected to fall from 87% to about 75%. GPU systems still make up roughly 60% of one large cloud's build, so displacement is partial rather than complete.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether in-house chips can handle training and newer model shapes, not just steady inference work.

falsifiableTrigger: gpuSpotPrice for H100 or GB200 drops more than 20% within a quarter.
mechanism: Renters bid up whatever is scarce, so prices hold while parts are allocated and soften only where older hardware becomes plentiful.
rationale: Rental prices for the newest systems are climbing, with the median hourly rate for the top rack-scale part up about 42% over a year and older parts still 24% above their November 2025 low, and NVIDIA held a 75.0% gross margin with the same level guided for the next quarter. But quoted median rates for the prior-generation H100 vary widely across trackers, from about $3.85 down to $2.97 per GPU-hour within a week, so price firmness is clear at the leading edge and looser for older parts.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to how quickly the newest racks reach rental fleets, since that is what turns today's scarce part into tomorrow's discounted one.

falsifiableTrigger: exportControlExposure eases so China DC revenue recovers above prior levels within two quarters.
mechanism: Government rules bar the strongest parts from a large buying market, so a share of world demand simply cannot be served no matter how much supply exists.
rationale: NVIDIA's China revenue fell to $4,550 million from $9,659 million a year earlier, it recorded no data-center Hopper shipments to China, licensed H200 shipments remain trivial despite about $10 billion of approved licences and carry a 25% import tariff, and NVIDIA more than halved the number of authorised Asian buyers under a new compliance list. AMD faces parallel restrictions and took about $440 million of related charges.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to policy changes in Washington and Beijing, which can reopen or reclose the market faster than any supply decision.

falsifiableTrigger: Vendor-financed GPU commitments in rpoBacklog exceed 300,000 units within two quarters.
mechanism: When the seller lends the money or guarantees the rent, reported orders partly reflect the seller's own credit rather than independent buyer budgets.
rationale: NVIDIA has scaled a programme that backstops smaller clouds' purchases, takes a share of their revenue and promises to rent back idle machines, covering about 210,000 accelerators at Firmus and Sharon AI on top of earlier support for CoreWeave and Lambda, and it raised $25 billion of bonds to fund it. Reporting this cycle also describes a discussed $350 billion facility for one model provider's chip purchases plus up to $250 billion of backstop for its data-center leases, and an undisclosed NVIDIA investment alongside a new frontier-lab commitment.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to the rental income of the financed buyers, because a shortfall there turns guarantees into real costs for the chip vendor.

falsifiableTrigger: customerConcentration for the top three direct customers falls below prior shares next fiscal year.
mechanism: A handful of buyers place most of the orders, so one of them slowing down or switching to its own chips removes a large slice of revenue at once.
rationale: NVIDIA disclosed three direct customers at 21%, 17% and 16% of total revenue in its latest quarter, up from a prior-year pattern where the four largest were already more than half of sales, and its backstop and revenue-share arrangements push more demand toward a small set of vendor-financed clouds. One of those large buyers is simultaneously putting its own in-house accelerators into production.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to how quickly sovereign, enterprise and neocloud buyers grow large enough to dilute the top few accounts.

falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA DC Ethernet switch market-share-pct slips from #1 within two quarters.
mechanism: Selling the switches and cabling with the accelerators makes the whole cluster one purchase, which raises the cost of swapping in another vendor's chips.
rationale: NVIDIA became the revenue leader in data-center Ethernet switching for the first time on the back of networking bundled with its newest accelerators, and its next switch generation already names CoreWeave, Microsoft, Nebius, SpaceXAI and Tesla as first deployers, with claimed 5x better power efficiency across clusters above 100,000 accelerators. No finding compares networking growth against compute growth, so the stronger claim that networking outgrows compute is still unsupported.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether open Ethernet fabrics from rival vendors reach the same cluster performance at lower cost.

falsifiableTrigger: Cost-per-token gains stall so tokenEconomics improves less than one generation cycle.
mechanism: Each generation lowers the price of serving a unit of model output, which makes uses that were too expensive worth running and lifts total compute bought.
rationale: The newest NVIDIA rack is reported to cut inference cost per token by about 10x versus the prior generation and to deliver ten times more work per megawatt, open-model serving costs have fallen 30% to 50% a year since 2023, and one large enterprise now burns roughly a trillion tokens a month. Cheaper tokens are showing up alongside more token consumption, not less.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether cheaper serving actually converts into new paid workloads rather than just lower bills on existing ones.

falsifiableTrigger: Prepaid HBM commitments in rpoBacklog shrink or deposits are refunded within a quarter.
mechanism: Buyers who put cash down years ahead on non-cancellable memory contracts have already paid for future accelerators, so that demand is committed rather than merely forecast.
rationale: Micron has signed 16 non-cancelable five-year take-or-pay agreements backed by more than $22 billion of cash and related commitments, including nearly $18 billion of cash deposits, memory suppliers have pre-sold their entire 2026 output under non-cancellable contracts at high-teen to low-twenties percent price increases, and NVIDIA signed a long-term supply and joint-development partnership with SK hynix. Large cloud buyers have separately locked long-term memory contracts with their own cash.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to the financial health of the depositing buyers, since only a solvent buyer's prepayment is a real lock.

falsifiableTrigger: exportControlExposure changes lift the sub-50% China cap or clear Blackwell within two quarters.
mechanism: Licences are granted one buyer at a time under a volume cap and a tariff, so the market reopens as a trickle rather than as a return to prior sales.
rationale: The January rule shifting H200-class chips from denial to case-by-case review still stands, with a 25% tariff and a cap holding China exports under half of comparable US sales, about ten Chinese firms cleared for up to 75,000 chips each and roughly $10 billion of licences approved, and first shipments have begun. Volumes remain trivial, the newest generation is still banned, China revenue sits at $4,550 million, and NVIDIA more than halved its authorised Asian buyer list, so the ceiling is unchanged.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the newest generation is ever cleared, since the licensed parts are a generation behind what buyers want.

falsifiableTrigger: AMD or non-NVIDIA designWins in production inference keep expanding for two consecutive quarters.
mechanism: Customers stay with one vendor only while porting their software costs more than the hardware saving, and that porting cost is falling as rival software stacks improve.
rationale: Anthropic committed to up to 2 gigawatts of AMD accelerators and OpenAI, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle are named on AMD's production racks, AMD reports its software stack delivering 3.3x inference and 2.4x training gains over the prior release plus a 2.10x throughput improvement on a leading open model, and a 1.6-trillion-parameter model was pretrained entirely on non-NVIDIA hardware. Frontier customers are now running real production work off NVIDIA's software.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to training work rather than inference, since training is where the software gap is still widest.

falsifiableTrigger: Memory hbmSupplyCapex expansion pulls DRAM/NVMe prices down within two quarters.
mechanism: Memory and flash are a large and rising share of what an AI server costs, so their price increases flow straight into the bill buyers pay per rack.
rationale: Rack component costs are inflating about 2% to 3% a week and sit 10% to 15% above baseline on memory and flash scarcity, memory component lead times have stretched to 32 to 40-plus weeks with prices up about 90% since late 2025, server memory contract prices are expected to rise more than 25% in the third quarter, and next-generation stacked memory contract prices are forecast to roughly double into 2027. Suppliers have cut quote validity to 72 hours.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether buyers pass the cost on or absorb it, which decides whether it hits budgets or system-builder margins.

falsifiableTrigger: releaseCadence slips push a major vendor's 2H-2026 ramp into 2027.
mechanism: Several vendors start volume production of new accelerators in the same window, but each ramps at its own pace, so total supply rises in steps spread across a year.
rationale: ADJUSTED: NVIDIA's newest racks ramp into production from the third quarter of 2026 while AMD's rack-scale volume mostly arrives in 2027, so the multi-vendor supply wave lands in stages rather than all at once. Supply-chain reporting still has NVIDIA, AMD, AWS and Google parts entering mass production together and AMD's rack reached production with third-quarter shipments, but one account puts AMD's real volume ramp and first production output at the second quarter of 2027 because of manufacturing delays, and Meta's in-house parts only enter production in September.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to packaging and memory allocation, because a ramp date means little if the parts to fill it are not available.

falsifiableTrigger: AMD customerConcentration eases as its buyer base broadens over the next two quarters.
mechanism: A few named partners account for nearly all of AMD's accelerator commitments, so its growth path rises or falls with those individual decisions.
rationale: AMD's disclosed pipeline runs through a short list of very large commitments: Anthropic at up to 2 gigawatts, OpenAI at 6 gigawatts, Meta at up to 6 gigawatts, plus Microsoft and Oracle, and AMD itself says it depends on a small number of customers and expects that to continue. Its own product launch disclosed no order quantities or revenue guidance, and the one broadening deal this cycle, a phased 30 megawatt rollout with Rackspace, is small next to the gigawatt-scale names.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the gigawatt commitments convert into shipped and paid volume on the stated schedule.

falsifiableTrigger: Crescent Island releaseCadence slips its customer sampling past the 2H 2026 quarter.
mechanism: Using ordinary memory on a simpler package skips the two scarcest steps in accelerator manufacturing, so output is not limited by the same queues.
rationale: Intel's inference chip still uses standard low-power memory rather than stacked memory specifically to avoid contention for advanced packaging and stacked memory, and it remains guided to customer sampling in the second half of 2026 with up to 480 gigabytes of onboard memory. Nothing this cycle shows shipped volume or a customer, so the route exists on paper but is not yet proven.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether ordinary memory bandwidth is enough for the inference work customers actually want to run.

falsifiableTrigger: TSMC grossMargin declines for two consecutive quarters as capacity loosens.
mechanism: When many different chip types compete for the same fab and packaging slots, the foundry can fill every line and charge more for each one.
rationale: TSMC reported a 67.7% gross margin, up 9.1 points from a year earlier, with revenue up 36% and full-year growth guidance raised from over 30% to above 40%, and it lifted 2026 capital spending by about $10 billion to $60-64 billion. Trade reporting says AI demand is spreading beyond accelerators into custom chips, networking and power parts, tightening both older and leading-edge lines as well as packaging, and TSMC says packaging scarcity is now limiting customer growth.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to a slowdown in any one large customer segment, which would free capacity and weaken pricing quickly.

falsifiableTrigger: A hyperscalerCapexRevision cuts 2026 or 2027 AI capex guidance within two quarters.
mechanism: Cloud buyers are spending far ahead of the revenue the new capacity earns, so a disappointing payback would force them to cut orders rather than keep building.
rationale: Alphabet raised 2026 capital spending to $195-205 billion, funded the quarter with $49.6 billion of equity and $20.3 billion of notes, and reported its first ever negative free cash flow of $5.9 billion; its shares fell about 6% on the day and other AI-linked names fell with it, which reads as investors treating the bigger budget as cost rather than growth. The four largest US buyers are on track for about $725 billion this year, up 77%, and analysts have publicly questioned whether that pace is sustainable.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to cloud revenue growth, which is the visible proof that the spending is earning its keep.

falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA grossMargin guidance drops below 70% in a coming quarter.
mechanism: Customers accept NVIDIA's prices because the alternatives are scarce or slower to deploy, which lets it keep a wide margin even through the costly early phase of a new product.
rationale: NVIDIA held a 75.0% non-GAAP gross margin and guided the following quarter to the same level while ramping new products, against AMD at 55% with about 56% guided and Intel at 40.4% rising to about 41%. The gap to rivals is roughly twenty points and did not narrow.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to memory and packaging input costs, which are rising fast and are the likeliest squeeze on the margin.

falsifiableTrigger: Top-buyer customerConcentration in CoWoS output falls below 85% within a year.
mechanism: A handful of customers book nearly all the advanced-packaging output, so if one steps back there is no queue of other buyers ready to take those slots at the same price.
rationale: The top three advanced-packaging customers account for more than 85% of TSMC's output, with NVIDIA at about 60% or roughly 595,000 wafers and AMD at about 11% or roughly 105,000 wafers. AMD must split its small allocation between server processors and accelerators, so every slot used for one takes capacity from the other.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to custom-chip designers growing their own packaging bookings, which would spread the customer base.

falsifiableTrigger: Aggregate rpoBacklog duration shortens as new commitments turn shorter-dated over two quarters.
mechanism: Buyers who fear being shut out sign longer contracts to reserve future capacity, which pushes the average delivery date of the order book further out.
rationale: Google Cloud's committed backlog rose by more than $50 billion in a quarter to $514 billion with just over half expected to convert within 24 months, meaning nearly half converts later than that; CoreWeave holds a $21 billion purchase commitment running through 2032, memory suppliers signed five-year take-or-pay contracts with order books extending into 2028, and NVIDIA is negotiating more than $750 billion of multi-year infrastructure agreements.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to how enforceable the long-dated commitments are if a buyer's own demand weakens.

falsifiableTrigger: A leading model provider reports revenue (apiArr) growth stalling quarter over quarter while compute commitments keep growing.
mechanism: Model providers can only keep buying compute if paying customers keep growing, so their sales figures are the test of whether the buildout rests on real revenue.
rationale: The only revenue figure in this cycle's findings is Anthropic reaching more than $30 billion of annual run-rate as of April 2026, which is not new, and the supporting evidence is qualitative: its compute chief says access to compute is what keeps its models at the frontier, its models are now generally available in Microsoft's platform on the newest hardware, and one enterprise customer is consuming about a trillion tokens a month. Real usage keeps growing, but no fresh sales figures arrived to raise conviction.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to disclosure, since these are private companies and the evidence arrives late and unevenly.

falsifiableTrigger: Chinese domestic accelerator designWins for frontier training stall over the next two quarters.
mechanism: With the strongest imported chips barred, Chinese buyers fund domestic suppliers, whose revenue and capability grow because there is no alternative.
rationale: Beyond the earlier capability proof of a 1.6-trillion-parameter model pretrained on more than 50,000 domestic accelerators across over 35 trillion tokens, Chinese suppliers now show volume: Moore Threads guided first-half revenue up 135.1% to 149.4% and Hygon up 55.6% to 70.2%. Chinese firms still ordered more than two million restricted NVIDIA parts for this year against roughly 700,000 units of inventory, and Chinese labs' own custom chips are judged more than two years away, so displacement is growing but incomplete.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to domestic memory and packaging supply, which caps how many domestic accelerators can actually be built.

falsifiableTrigger: A neocloud's marginalBuyerFinancing debt load or net loss narrows for two consecutive quarters.
mechanism: These operators buy accelerators years before the rental income arrives, so faster growth means bigger upfront costs and wider losses at the same time.
rationale: CoreWeave's full-year revenue grew about 168% from $1.9 billion to $5.1 billion while its net loss widened from $937 million to $1.2 billion, and it raised 2026 capital spending to $31-35 billion, roughly double the $14.9 billion spent last year. Total debt rose 16.1% in a single quarter to $24.86 billion.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to rental price levels, since a drop would push the payback on already-bought fleets further out.

falsifiableTrigger: A top hyperscaler cuts its 2027 gigawatt power target below its 2026 level.
mechanism: An accelerator only earns money once it is plugged into a powered building, so available electricity and grid equipment set the real deployment ceiling.
rationale: Gartner projects 40% of AI data centers will be power-constrained by 2027 as global data-center electricity roughly doubles from about 485 to about 950 terawatt-hours, and power transformer lead times average 128 weeks, reaching 200 weeks for specialty units, with prices up 77% since 2019. Buyers now describe their plans in power terms: Meta at 7 gigawatts this year and roughly double next year, Anthropic at 2 gigawatts of AMD hardware, a Japanese national site at 140 megawatts and an Indonesian campus at 360 megawatts.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to gains in work done per megawatt, which stretch a fixed power budget across more compute.

falsifiableTrigger: Broadcom-plus-Marvell market-share-pct of custom ASIC co-design falls below 90% within a year.
mechanism: Cloud firms design the chip idea but hand the hard engineering to outside partners, so the escape route from merchant GPUs runs through the same two firms.
rationale: Broadcom and Marvell together are estimated to hold about 95% of the custom AI chip co-design market, and Broadcom alone carries a $73 billion order book with a target of $100 billion of annual AI chip revenue by 2027. The only sign of broadening is early-stage talk between Anthropic and Samsung about a custom chip on a 2 nanometre process, which is not yet a competing design house.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether a third design partner or an in-house team lands a large production programme.

falsifiableTrigger: Wistron odmMonthlyAiRevenue falls year-over-year for two consecutive months.
mechanism: Contract manufacturers bill only when finished servers leave the factory, so their monthly sales are a direct read on machines actually shipping.
rationale: Wistron posted record June revenue of NT$321.82 billion, up 53.9% from a year earlier and 10.9% from the prior month, on AI-server and networking shipments, and it opened a new 324,000 square-foot plant in Texas to build NVIDIA systems. Supply-chain firms report the order boom spilling into the second half of the year.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to component shortages, since a memory or packaging gap stops the line regardless of order intake.

falsifiableTrigger: A neocloud's marginalBuyerFinancing debt-to-equity rises above 6:1 within two quarters.
mechanism: Accelerator fleets are bought with borrowed money against future rental contracts, so the equity cushion stays thin while the debt grows with each purchase.
rationale: CoreWeave has raised $18.81 billion of debt against $3.5 billion of equity, a 5.4 to 1 ratio, with total debt of $24.86 billion up 16.1% in one quarter, while raising 2026 capital spending to $31-35 billion. NVIDIA is separately backstopping smaller operators' purchases, which substitutes vendor credit for equity rather than reducing leverage.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to borrowing costs and to how long rented hardware keeps its earning power.

falsifiableTrigger: Co-packaged optics adoption stalls below 5% of AI optical modules through 2027.
mechanism: Putting the optics inside the switch package moves cluster wiring onto the semiconductor supply chain, so networking capacity now depends on packaging lines rather than pluggable module vendors.
rationale: Co-packaged optics is projected to grow from about 0.5% of AI optical modules this year to about 35% by 2030, with NVIDIA's photonics switches due in the second half of 2026 and an earlier model already shipping, and Taiwanese packaging houses are newly competing for silicon photonics work as the technology enters commercial use. NVIDIA claims 5x better power efficiency from its photonics Ethernet across clusters above 100,000 accelerators.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to packaging capacity, because the same lines are already stretched by accelerator demand.

falsifiableTrigger: A named US fab or packaging project slips its build milestone past 2027.
mechanism: Building fabrication, packaging and assembly inside the United States adds capacity that does not depend on a single island, which widens the supply base over time.
rationale: NVIDIA plans up to $500 billion of AI infrastructure production in the United States with TSMC, Foxconn, Wistron, Corning, Lumentum, Coherent and Amkor, Wistron opened a 324,000 square-foot plant in Texas, Micron committed $250 billion to US memory manufacturing through 2035 targeting 40% of its output domestically and broke ground in New York, and TSMC announced an incremental $100 billion US investment. Commitments are large but mostly still construction rather than output.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to construction and equipment timelines, since announced dollars only matter once a line is running.

falsifiableTrigger: Google Cloud or CoreWeave rpoBacklog fails to grow sequentially for two consecutive quarters.
mechanism: Providers cannot deliver contracts faster than they can build capacity, so signed commitments show demand earlier and more fully than reported sales do.
rationale: Google Cloud's committed backlog rose more than $50 billion in one quarter to $514 billion from $462 billion, far outpacing quarterly revenue of $24.8 billion even as that revenue accelerated to 82% growth with operating income of $8.8 billion versus $2.8 billion a year earlier. CoreWeave's contracted backlog reached $99.4 billion against full-year revenue of $5.1 billion, and supply-chain firms report orders spilling into the second half.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to how much of the backlog is cancellable, since soft commitments would overstate real demand.

falsifiableTrigger: A top hyperscaler returns to positive free cash flow while holding 2027 capex guidance for two consecutive quarters.
mechanism: Building capacity now costs more than these businesses generate in cash, so the gap is filled with borrowed money and new shares.
rationale: Alphabet funded its latest quarter with $49.6 billion of equity issuance and $20.3 billion of senior unsecured notes and reported its first ever negative free cash flow of $5.9 billion, while raising 2026 capital spending to $195-205 billion. The four largest US buyers are heading for about $725 billion of capital spending this year, up 77% from about $410 billion.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to credit conditions, because dearer borrowing would force spending discipline quickly.

falsifiableTrigger: A new accelerator generation delivers less than a 1.5x perfPerWatt gain over its predecessor.
mechanism: Each generation does more work for the same electricity, so a buyer with a fixed power budget can keep adding capability without adding megawatts.
rationale: NVIDIA's newest rack is claimed to deliver ten times the throughput per megawatt of the prior generation, an enterprise deployment claims up to ten times the performance per megawatt of the equipment it replaces, and its photonics networking claims five times better power efficiency. Independent measurement is more modest, putting the prior generational step at about 1.6 times, so the direction holds while the size of the gain depends on the source.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to vendor claims versus measured results, since much of the evidence comes from the sellers.

falsifiableTrigger: HBM leadTimes shorten and suppliers report unsold capacity for two consecutive quarters before end-2027.
mechanism: Every accelerator needs a fixed number of memory stacks, so once memory output is fully sold the number of accelerators that can be finished is fixed too.
rationale: Micron says its stacked-memory shipment growth is capped by supply rather than end demand, with 2027-2028 customer demand far above what it can supply and order books running into 2028, and Morgan Stanley sees no sign the shortage is easing and flags the risk it intensifies in 2027 and 2028. SK hynix's chief expects constraints to persist through 2027, memory component lead times have stretched to 32 to 40-plus weeks, and 2026 output is fully pre-sold with only 50% to 66% of one supplier's customer demand met.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to new memory fab output arriving, since stacked memory uses about three times the wafer capacity of standard memory.

falsifiableTrigger: Memory supplier gross margin falls for two consecutive quarters as contract prices flatten.
mechanism: Memory suppliers are the scarce link in the chain, so they set prices and keep more of the value in each AI server for themselves.
rationale: Micron's data-center segment reported $11.5 billion of revenue, up 103% in a single quarter, at an 87% gross margin, which is above the chip vendors it supplies; next-generation stacked memory contract prices are forecast to roughly double into 2027, server memory contract prices are expected to rise more than 25% in the third quarter, and one supplier is seeking up to a 20% contract increase. Server builders absorb those increases in their costs.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to new memory capacity, which historically turns extraordinary margins into ordinary ones fast.

falsifiableTrigger: No new sovereign or enterprise cluster above 10,000 GPUs is announced for two consecutive quarters.
mechanism: Governments and large firms are buying whole clusters of their own rather than renting, which adds a buyer group that sits outside the big cloud operators.
rationale: A Japanese national project with the trade ministry will deploy 27,500 next-generation NVIDIA accelerators and 13,750 processors across 140 megawatts, an Indonesian campus will run up to 170,000 accelerators across 360 megawatts, SK Group signed a partnership described as above $500 billion covering AI factories, Bristol Myers Squibb is deploying a second eight-system cluster, AT&T is running about a trillion tokens a month, and AMD launched a product line aimed specifically at sovereign and scientific buyers.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to public budgets and political commitment, which move on slower and less predictable cycles than cloud spending.

falsifiableTrigger: Intel data-center revenue growth falls below 10% year over year for two consecutive quarters.
mechanism: Intel is winning back server processor sales and outside manufacturing work at improving margins, which puts a third supplier back into the AI hardware chain.
rationale: Intel's data-center and AI revenue reached $6.3 billion, up 59% from a year earlier with $2.5 billion of operating income, its foundry revenue reached $5.8 billion, up 31% on better yields and faster cycle times, gross margin rose to 40.4% from 27.5% with about 41% guided, and it guided next-quarter revenue of $15.8-16.8 billion above the $15.1 billion expected. It also raised capital spending above $20 billion, added Fortinet as a named external foundry customer and committed EUR 5 billion to expand its Irish campus.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether its newest process reaches volume yields, since the foundry recovery rests on that.

falsifiableTrigger: New vendor equity-for-compute deals in marginalBuyerFinancing stop appearing for two consecutive quarters.
mechanism: Chip vendors put their own money into the firms that buy their chips, so part of reported demand is funded by the seller rather than by outside investors.
rationale: AMD committed a strategic equity investment of up to $5 billion in Anthropic alongside a 2 gigawatt compute deal, NVIDIA made an undisclosed investment in Safe Superintelligence alongside that lab's commitment to its next platform, NVIDIA is separately taking revenue shares from startups in exchange for access to more than 200,000 accelerators, and it agreed to buy $5 billion of Intel stock alongside a custom processor arrangement. The pattern now covers both merchant vendors.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the funded customers raise independent capital, which would show the demand stands on its own.

falsifiableTrigger: Standard DRAM S10 spot prices fall for two consecutive months as suppliers restore non-AI capacity.
mechanism: Memory makers shift their lines to the highest-priced AI parts, which starves ordinary memory buyers and lifts prices on everyday products.
rationale: AMD is raising graphics card bundle prices about 10%, with channel reports of 10% to 15%, citing tight memory and graphics memory spot prices that have roughly tripled since late 2025; older standard memory hit $81.20, up 17.5% in a month and above its previous peak, newer standard memory broke $50 for the first time, and suppliers are cutting standard and embedded output to favour AI parts. Enterprise contracts are also getting priority on flash allocation, squeezing consumer drives.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to when new fabrication capacity comes online, since none is expected before late 2026.

falsifiableTrigger: No new multi-year accelerator-to-memory supply partnership is announced for two consecutive quarters through 2027.
mechanism: Accelerator makers contract directly with memory suppliers because reserved memory output is what determines how many chips they can finish.
rationale: NVIDIA entered a long-term partnership with SK hynix to secure next-generation memory supply and jointly develop it, inside a wider arrangement with SK Group described as above $500 billion, and all three major memory makers have begun full-scale development of a 16-layer next-generation stack specifically for NVIDIA targeting delivery by the fourth quarter of 2026. Memory suppliers have separately signed 16 five-year take-or-pay contracts backed by roughly $18 billion of cash deposits.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether these reservations displace other buyers or simply reprice the same limited output.

falsifiableTrigger: The leading supplier's HBM market-share-pct falls below 50% within four quarters as rivals ship volume.
mechanism: One supplier makes most of the stacked memory and the biggest buyers have booked its output, so whoever holds a contract with that supplier can build AI servers and others cannot.
rationale: SK Hynix still holds 56.4% of the stacked-memory market and approved a 7.09 trillion won, about $4.83 billion, packaging plant to expand capacity, while Microsoft, Google and Meta have used their cash to lock long-term supply, keeping access concentrated at the top. But rivals are moving: Samsung is reported to be raising capacity 50% this year, Micron is scaling its own output, and all three are developing the next-generation stack for NVIDIA, so single-source dominance holds without deepening.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether rival suppliers qualify their next-generation stacks at the same yields and dates.

falsifiableTrigger: No new diversion prosecution or whitelist reduction is reported for two consecutive quarters.
mechanism: Prosecutions and shorter approved-buyer lists raise the personal and commercial cost of reselling restricted chips, which shuts the informal channels that used to carry them.
rationale: Taiwanese prosecutors expanded a criminal smuggling probe, raiding Super Micro's Taiwan office and affiliated sites and detaining employees, tied to US charges alleging about $2.5 billion of servers were shipped to China without a licence. NVIDIA separately more than halved the number of Asian customers authorised to buy its AI chips under a new compliance list.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to enforcement outside Taiwan, since routes can shift to jurisdictions with less scrutiny.

falsifiableTrigger: CoWoS lead times stay above 52 weeks through the end of 2027 while the supply gap fails to narrow below 15%.
mechanism: Packaging capacity can be added by building more lines and hiring outside assembly partners, while memory needs new fabs and long production cycles, so packaging loosens first.
rationale: ADJUSTED: Advanced-packaging capacity is expanding fast enough to narrow the shortfall from about 20% to about 10% by the end of 2026, but lead times stay at 52 to 78 weeks with bookings into 2027 and TSMC says the demand gap runs through 2029-2030, so packaging eases only slowly while memory stays the tighter of the two limits. Capacity is rising toward 125,000 to 130,000 wafers a month, could approach 200,000 including outside assembly partners, and outside packaging houses are adding capacity while NVIDIA weighs moving some output to Intel's packaging, yet memory shows no easing at all with suppliers warning of tightness through 2027 and into 2028.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to how much packaging each new accelerator generation consumes, since bigger parts can absorb the added capacity.

falsifiableTrigger: NAND contract prices for server drives fall for two consecutive quarters while Rubin deployments keep growing.
mechanism: The newest racks hold far more flash storage per system, so each one shipped consumes a large block of an industry that was not sized for it.
rationale: The newest NVIDIA generation adds a large storage tier expected to pull flash demand from about 35 million terabytes this year to more than 100 million terabytes next year, with each unit carrying 576 drives for 9,600 terabytes, described as adding demand the size of a major consumer electronics maker. Enterprise contracts are already getting priority allocation over retail, and rack component costs are rising 2% to 3% a week on memory and flash scarcity.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to how fast the newest generation actually deploys, since the demand step only lands with those racks.

falsifiableTrigger: Public list rates for the newest rack-scale systems appear on major provider pricing pages within two quarters.
mechanism: When the newest systems are scarce, providers sell them through negotiation instead of a list price so they can charge what each buyer will pay.
rationale: CoreWeave's live page lists hourly rates for last-generation eight-accelerator nodes at $49.24 and $68.80 but shows no rate for its newest systems, which are quoted only through sales, and Lambda lists no rate for two current parts with longer terms quoted as custom pricing and carries no AMD instances at all. One provider does still publish a rate for a current rack-scale system at $42.00 per four-accelerator instance, so the pattern is strong rather than absolute.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to supply of the newest racks, since published prices tend to return once a part is no longer allocated.

detail.falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA accelerator market-share-pct stabilises or rises for 2 consecutive quarters while rival shipments grow.
detail.mechanism: The total market is growing faster than NVIDIA can supply, so rivals absorb the overflow and gain share while NVIDIA's own sales keep rising.
detail.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether NVIDIA's supply constraints ease, because a vendor that can ship everything buyers want stops leaking share.
detail.statement: NVIDIA's share of AI accelerators is falling even as its revenue sets records, so rivals are taking growth rather than taking business away.
detail.title: NVIDIA's share slips while its sales still grow

detail.falsifiableTrigger: A major buyer returns to purchasing loose accelerators rather than vendor racks for a flagship cluster within 2 quarters.
detail.mechanism: Selling a finished rack bundles chips, networking, cooling and software into one decision, which shifts competition from chip specifications to whole-system output per dollar and per megawatt.
detail.sensitivity: Most sensitive to open rack standards, which would let buyers mix vendors again and undo the bundling.
detail.statement: Both merchant vendors now sell whole 72-accelerator racks with their own networking and software rather than individual chips, so buyers compare complete systems instead of parts.
detail.title: The rack, not the chip, is now the unit of competition

detail.falsifiableTrigger: Power transformer lead times fall below 80 weeks for 2 consecutive quarters.
detail.mechanism: A site cannot energise without transformers and switchgear that take two to four years to arrive, so ordering that equipment sets the earliest date accelerators can be plugged in.
detail.sensitivity: Most sensitive to transformer factory expansion, which is slow and serves many industries beyond data centers.
detail.statement: Power transformers and similar grid equipment now take years to deliver, so new AI sites are held up by electrical gear rather than by chips.
detail.title: Grid equipment lead times gate new AI sites

detail.falsifiableTrigger: Median newest-generation gpuSpotPrice falls while prior-generation rates rise for 2 consecutive months.
detail.mechanism: Buyers pay up for whatever is scarce and fast, so as older hardware becomes plentiful its rate falls while the newest systems command a rising premium.
detail.sensitivity: Most sensitive to how fast the newest racks reach rental fleets, which is what eventually turns today's premium part into a discounted one.
detail.statement: Rental prices for the newest systems are rising while quotes for the previous generation spread out and drift lower, so the price premium is concentrating in whatever just launched.
detail.title: The rental premium moves to the newest hardware

falsifiableTrigger: B200 rpoBacklog falls below 2 million units for two consecutive quarters.
mechanism: Buyers keep committing to more accelerators than NVIDIA can build, so orders pile up faster than the company can ship them.
rationale: NVIDIA posted record quarterly data-center revenue of $75.2 billion, up 92% year over year, and guided the next quarter to $91.0 billion, while an order book of roughly 3.6 million of its top rack part and more than $750 billion of infrastructure agreements sit ahead of it, and its memory supplier says accelerator shipments are capped by supply rather than by end demand.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the largest cloud buyers keep raising their spending plans rather than pausing them.

falsifiableTrigger: HBM leadTimes ease to available-on-demand and CoWoS lead times fall below 26 weeks before the end of 2027.
mechanism: Two scarce inputs, stacked memory and advanced packaging, set a hard ceiling on how many accelerators anyone can finish and ship.
rationale: Stacked memory is sold out through 2026 with much of 2027 pre-booked and no sign of easing, while TSMC's advanced packaging is fully booked with 52 to 78 week waits and bookings running into 2027 even as monthly capacity climbs toward 130,000 wafers.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to how fast memory makers add capacity, since packaging is expanding faster than memory.

falsifiableTrigger: AMD accelerator market-share-pct fails to rise above 7% through 2027.
mechanism: Named multi-gigawatt commitments from the largest AI buyers turn AMD's product plans into shipped volume that takes real share.
rationale: AMD put its 72-accelerator rack into production with shipments starting in the third quarter and named Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle as adopters, and its data-center revenue rose 57% year over year, although its accelerator share is still only about 5 to 7% against NVIDIA at roughly 80%.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether AMD's rack volume arrives in 2026 or slips into 2027 as one supply-chain account suggests.

falsifiableTrigger: ASIC market-share-pct growth falls back below GPU growth for two consecutive quarters.
mechanism: Large buyers move part of their inference work onto chips they design themselves, which takes growth away from chips bought on the open market.
rationale: Forecasters put custom-chip growth at 44.6% for 2026 against 16.1% for merchant graphics processors, custom silicon spending is projected to move from $8 billion in 2024 to over $25 billion in 2026, and Meta's own four inference parts enter production in September 2026.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether in-house parts stay captive to their creators instead of being rented to outside customers.

falsifiableTrigger: gpuSpotPrice for H100 or GB200 drops more than 20% within a quarter.
mechanism: Renters bid up scarce accelerator hours because new capacity arrives more slowly than the work waiting to run on it.
rationale: Median rental for NVIDIA's top rack part rose about 42% over the year to $18.77 per hour, its two prior parts each rose about 11%, and one tracker reports rental prices up 24% from their November 2025 low.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to how much rental capacity lands when several vendors ramp new racks at once.

falsifiableTrigger: exportControlExposure eases so China DC revenue recovers above prior levels within two quarters.
mechanism: Government licence rules cut off a large block of buyers, so a share of real demand simply cannot be served.
rationale: NVIDIA's China revenue fell to $4,550 million from $9,659 million a year earlier with no top-line data-center shipments in the quarter, licences granted since February 2026 have produced no revenue, the company assumes no China compute revenue in its outlook, and it more than halved the list of Asian customers cleared to buy.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether approved licences turn into actual shipments rather than staying on paper.

falsifiableTrigger: Vendor-financed GPU commitments in rpoBacklog exceed 300,000 units within two quarters.
mechanism: NVIDIA lends or guarantees the money its customers use to buy its own chips, so part of its reported demand depends on credit it extends itself.
rationale: NVIDIA's backstop programme now covers about 210,000 accelerators across two early partners, it raised $25 billion of bonds in June 2026 to fund the programme, and it is discussing a $350 billion facility for one customer's chip purchases plus a backstop of that customer's data-centre debt.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the financed buyers can refinance on their own terms once these deals mature.

falsifiableTrigger: customerConcentration for the top three direct customers falls below prior shares next fiscal year.
mechanism: A handful of buyers account for most of the revenue, so one of them slowing orders would move the whole number.
rationale: NVIDIA disclosed three direct customers at 21%, 17% and 16% of quarterly revenue, and for the prior fiscal year one customer was 22% and another 14%, up from three customers at about 11 to 12% the year before, with the four largest now more than half of revenue.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether sovereign and enterprise buyers grow fast enough to dilute the top few accounts.

falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA DC Ethernet switch market-share-pct slips from #1 within two quarters.
mechanism: Selling the switches and the accelerators together makes it harder for a buyer to swap out one part without rebuilding the whole cluster.
rationale: NVIDIA took the top revenue spot in data-centre Ethernet switching for the first time on the back of networking bundled with its racks, and its newest switch generation launched with CoreWeave, Microsoft, Nebius, SpaceXAI and Tesla as first customers claiming five times better power efficiency across deployments above 100,000 accelerators.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether open networking standards let buyers mix vendors inside one rack.

falsifiableTrigger: Cost-per-token gains stall so tokenEconomics improves less than one generation cycle.
mechanism: Each price cut per unit of output makes more applications worth running, so total work bought on these chips grows even as the unit price falls.
rationale: The newest NVIDIA generation is reported to cut inference cost per token by about ten times against the prior generation, open-model serving costs have fallen 30 to 50% a year since 2023, and one telecom customer now burns roughly a trillion tokens a month.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether cheaper serving keeps creating new workloads instead of just shrinking existing bills.

falsifiableTrigger: Prepaid HBM commitments in rpoBacklog shrink or deposits are refunded within a quarter.
mechanism: Customers who have already paid cash for memory they cannot cancel will keep buying the accelerators that memory goes into.
rationale: Micron has signed sixteen non-cancelable five-year take-or-pay agreements backed by more than $22 billion of commitments including nearly $18 billion of cash deposits, and the whole industry's 2026 stacked-memory output is sold out under non-cancellable contracts with order books running into 2028.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether any large buyer walks away from a deposit rather than take delivery.

falsifiableTrigger: exportControlExposure changes lift the sub-50% China cap or clear Blackwell within two quarters.
mechanism: Case-by-case licences let a trickle of older parts into China while the volume cap and the ban on the newest parts hold the ceiling in place.
rationale: The reopening is now measurable and still tightly capped: about ten Chinese firms are cleared for up to 75,000 chips each against roughly $10 billion of approved licences, first shipments have begun but stay minimal, orders of more than two million units face inventory of about 700,000, the newest generation stays banned, and the rule keeps China exports under half of comparable United States sales with a roughly 25% tariff.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether approved licences convert into shipped units at any real scale.

falsifiableTrigger: AMD or non-NVIDIA designWins in production inference keep expanding for two consecutive quarters.
mechanism: Rival software stacks have improved enough that the largest buyers now run production work on non-NVIDIA chips, so software difficulty no longer holds them in place.
rationale: The named falsification has happened: non-NVIDIA production wins keep expanding, with Anthropic taking up to 2 gigawatts of AMD accelerators, OpenAI at 6 gigawatts and Microsoft, Meta and Oracle named as adopters, AMD reporting software speed-ups of 3.3 times in inference and 2.4 times in training, and a Chinese team pretraining a 1.6-trillion-parameter model on more than 50,000 domestic parts with no NVIDIA chips at all.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the announced gigawatt commitments actually run production traffic rather than staying pilots.

falsifiableTrigger: Memory hbmSupplyCapex expansion pulls DRAM/NVMe prices down within two quarters.
mechanism: Memory is a large share of an AI server's bill of materials, so every price rise lifts the cost of each machine a buyer installs.
rationale: Rack component costs are rising about 2 to 3% a week and sit 10 to 15% above baseline, memory component lead times have stretched to 32 to 40-plus weeks with prices up about 90% since late 2025, server memory contract prices are expected to rise more than 25% quarter over quarter, and stacked-memory contract prices are forecast to roughly double into 2027.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to how quickly new memory fabrication capacity comes online through 2027.

falsifiableTrigger: releaseCadence slips push a major vendor's 2H-2026 ramp into 2027.
mechanism: Each vendor hits production at a different date, so added supply arrives in steps rather than as one flood.
rationale: The staged picture held this cycle: NVIDIA's newest rack entered production ramp in the third quarter with wide cloud deployment, AMD's rack reached full production with third-quarter shipments but its real volume ramp runs into 2027, and Meta's own parts only enter production in September 2026.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to manufacturing delays at the vendor whose volume is furthest out.

falsifiableTrigger: AMD customerConcentration eases as its buyer base broadens over the next two quarters.
mechanism: A few very large contracts carry most of AMD's accelerator growth, so one buyer changing plans swings the whole line.
rationale: AMD's announced gigawatt-scale commitments sit with a short list of buyers, OpenAI at 6 gigawatts, Meta at up to 6 gigawatts, Anthropic at up to 2 gigawatts plus a July 2026 Microsoft expansion and a 50,000-accelerator Oracle cluster, and AMD itself says it expects continued customer concentration in revenue and receivables.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether mid-sized buyers such as the newly signed hosting and telecom accounts scale up.

falsifiableTrigger: Crescent Island releaseCadence slips its customer sampling past the 2H 2026 quarter.
mechanism: Using ordinary memory instead of the stacked kind lets a chip skip the two most congested steps in the supply chain.
rationale: Intel's inference part still targets customer sampling in the second half of 2026 and is described as using up to 480 gigabytes of standard low-power memory precisely to avoid competing for advanced packaging and stacked memory, with no slip reported this cycle.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the slower memory is fast enough for the inference work buyers actually run.

falsifiableTrigger: TSMC grossMargin declines for two consecutive quarters as capacity loosens.
mechanism: Demand arriving from many product families at once fills every kind of TSMC line, which lets the company charge more for scarce slots.
rationale: TSMC reported a 67.7% gross margin, up 9.1 percentage points, raised full-year growth guidance from over 30% to more than 40%, said its packaging capacity is so tight it limits customer growth with the gap running through 2029 and 2030, and reporting describes AI demand spreading beyond accelerators into custom chips, networking and power parts across both older and newer production lines.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to how much new capacity the current heavy capital spending brings online in 2027.

falsifiableTrigger: A hyperscalerCapexRevision cuts 2026 or 2027 AI capex guidance within two quarters.
mechanism: Spending is rising much faster than the cash these businesses generate, so a disappointing return would force buyers to cut orders.
rationale: The four largest cloud buyers plan about $725 billion of 2026 spending, up roughly 77%, yet Alphabet's shares fell about 6% on the day it raised its own guidance and it reported its first-ever negative free cash flow of $5.9 billion, while chip shares fell on spending jitters and analysts publicly questioned whether the jump is sustainable.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether cloud revenue keeps accelerating fast enough to justify the higher budgets.

falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA grossMargin guidance drops below 70% in a coming quarter.
mechanism: Buyers keep paying premium prices during a product changeover, which normally squeezes margins, so NVIDIA holds its pricing power.
rationale: NVIDIA reported a 75.0% adjusted gross margin and guided the next quarter to the same level even while ramping a new generation, against AMD at 55% and Intel at 41.8%.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to how much of the rising memory and component cost NVIDIA has to absorb rather than pass on.

falsifiableTrigger: Top-buyer customerConcentration in CoWoS output falls below 85% within a year.
mechanism: Because a few buyers hold nearly all the booked packaging slots, capacity freed by any one of them would be hard to fill quickly.
rationale: Two separate accounts put the top three advanced-packaging customers above 85% of TSMC output, with NVIDIA at roughly 60% or about 595,000 wafers and AMD at about 11% or 105,000 wafers, and NVIDIA booking more than half of the 2026 to 2027 expansion.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether smaller custom-chip programmes win packaging slots as capacity expands.

falsifiableTrigger: Aggregate rpoBacklog duration shortens as new commitments turn shorter-dated over two quarters.
mechanism: Buyers now sign multi-year commitments rather than near-term orders, so a rising share of demand is locked in long before delivery.
rationale: Google Cloud's backlog rose more than $50 billion in a quarter to $514 billion with only just over half expected to convert within 24 months, CoreWeave's contracted backlog reached $99.4 billion including a $21 billion Meta commitment running to 2032, and memory take-or-pay contracts now run five years.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether long-dated bookings convert on schedule rather than being renegotiated.

falsifiableTrigger: A leading model provider reports revenue (apiArr) growth stalling quarter over quarter while compute commitments keep growing.
mechanism: Model providers can only keep signing large compute contracts if their own sales keep growing fast enough to pay for them.
rationale: The one revenue data point this cycle still supports the claim, with Anthropic's annual recurring revenue above $30 billion as of April 2026 against $1 billion in January 2025, and its compute chief tying frontier work directly to access to chips, but no second provider's revenue is reported.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to how thin the reported evidence is, since it rests on a single provider's figure.

falsifiableTrigger: Chinese domestic accelerator designWins for frontier training stall over the next two quarters.
mechanism: Chinese buyers who cannot get NVIDIA parts shift spending to domestic suppliers, whose sales then grow quickly from a small base.
rationale: Capability evidence held with a 1.6-trillion-parameter model pretrained on more than 50,000 domestic parts, and volume evidence arrived for the first time as Moore Threads guided first-half revenue up 135 to 149% and Hygon up 56 to 70%, while Chinese orders of more than two million restricted NVIDIA parts still dwarf domestic output and in-house lab silicon is judged more than two years away.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether domestic suppliers can get enough memory and packaging to scale their own output.

falsifiableTrigger: A neocloud's marginalBuyerFinancing debt load or net loss narrows for two consecutive quarters.
mechanism: These operators buy fleets faster than the rental income arrives, so growth and losses rise together.
rationale: CoreWeave's revenue grew about 168% from $1.9 billion to $5.1 billion while its net loss widened from $937 million to $1.2 billion, and its total debt rose 16.1% in a single quarter to $24.86 billion.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to rental prices holding up long enough to cover the depreciation on newly bought fleets.

falsifiableTrigger: A top hyperscaler cuts its 2027 gigawatt power target below its 2026 level.
mechanism: Buyers now plan around the electricity they can secure, so available power sets how many accelerators they can install.
rationale: Gartner projects 40% of AI data centres will be power-constrained by 2027 as data-centre electricity roughly doubles from about 485 to about 950 terawatt-hours, Meta now sizes its plan as 7 gigawatts in 2026 and roughly double in 2027, and new sites are described in megawatts of capacity rather than chip counts.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to how fast new generation and grid connections are approved near data-centre sites.
