falsifiableTrigger: Broadcom-plus-Marvell market-share-pct of custom ASIC co-design falls below 90% within a year.
mechanism: Cloud buyers who design their own chips still hire the same two firms to do the engineering, so the alternative route has its own single point of failure.
rationale: The concentration figure is unchanged this cycle, with Broadcom and Marvell together estimated at about 95% of custom AI chip co-design, while Broadcom's $73 billion order book and $100 billion 2027 revenue target show how much volume runs through that narrow channel.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether buyers build in-house design teams or hire a third firm.

falsifiableTrigger: Wistron odmMonthlyAiRevenue falls year-over-year for two consecutive months.
mechanism: Contract manufacturers only book revenue when machines physically ship, so their monthly sales confirm that orders turn into hardware.
rationale: Wistron posted record June 2026 revenue of NT$321.82 billion, up 53.9% year over year and 10.9% on the month on AI-server and networking shipments, opened a 324,000-square-foot plant in Texas to build NVIDIA systems, and supply-chain reporting describes an order boom running into the second half of 2026.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to component shortages that could stall assembly even with orders in hand.

falsifiableTrigger: A neocloud's marginalBuyerFinancing debt-to-equity rises above 6:1 within two quarters.
mechanism: Borrowing pays for most of the fleet, so a thin equity cushion has to absorb any drop in rental income.
rationale: CoreWeave has raised $18.81 billion of debt against $3.5 billion of equity, a 5.4 to 1 ratio, with total debt of $24.86 billion up 16.1% in one quarter, while it roughly doubles its capital spending plan to $31 to 35 billion.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to credit conditions and to whether lenders keep accepting accelerators as collateral.

falsifiableTrigger: Co-packaged optics adoption stalls below 5% of AI optical modules through 2027.
mechanism: Putting the optics inside the switch package changes who builds cluster wiring and ties it to a fast-moving optics roadmap.
rationale: Co-packaged optics is projected to move from about 0.5% of AI optical modules in 2026 to about 35% by 2030 with NVIDIA's photonics switches arriving in 2026, the newest switch generation claims five times better power efficiency, and Taiwanese packaging houses are newly competing for silicon photonics work.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether packaging houses can produce these parts at acceptable yields.

falsifiableTrigger: A named US fab or packaging project slips its build milestone past 2027.
mechanism: Building fabrication and assembly capacity outside Taiwan adds a second place where the same hardware can be made.
rationale: NVIDIA plans up to $500 billion of AI infrastructure production in the United States with named partners, Wistron opened a Texas plant, Micron committed $250 billion to domestic memory manufacturing through 2035 and broke ground in New York, and TSMC announced an incremental $100 billion United States investment.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether these announcements turn into working plants on the stated timetable.

falsifiableTrigger: Google Cloud or CoreWeave rpoBacklog fails to grow sequentially for two consecutive quarters.
mechanism: Providers sign contracts faster than they can install capacity, so the order book shows demand earlier than the revenue line does.
rationale: Google Cloud's backlog jumped more than $50 billion in a quarter to $514 billion while its revenue grew 82% year over year, and CoreWeave's contracted backlog rose from $66.8 billion to $99.4 billion, so bookings are running well ahead of delivered sales.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to how much of the booked work converts inside two years rather than being pushed out.

falsifiableTrigger: A top hyperscaler returns to positive free cash flow while holding 2027 capex guidance for two consecutive quarters.
mechanism: Spending has outgrown the cash these businesses produce, so they now raise outside money to pay for capacity.
rationale: Alphabet funded its quarter with $49.6 billion of equity issuance and $20.3 billion of senior unsecured notes and reported its first-ever negative free cash flow of $5.9 billion, and the largest cloud buyers together plan about $725 billion of 2026 spending, up about 77%.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to borrowing costs and to investors' willingness to fund further issuance.

falsifiableTrigger: A new accelerator generation delivers less than a 1.5x perfPerWatt gain over its predecessor.
mechanism: More work per megawatt lets buyers add capacity inside a fixed power and packaging budget.
rationale: NVIDIA's newest rack is reported to deliver ten times the throughput per megawatt of the prior generation and its enterprise system ten times the performance per megawatt of what it replaces, with an independent measure putting the previous step at about 1.6 times and its photonics switching claiming five times better power efficiency.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether vendor efficiency claims hold up in independent measurement.

falsifiableTrigger: HBM leadTimes shorten and suppliers report unsold capacity for two consecutive quarters before end-2027.
mechanism: Every accelerator needs stacked memory it cannot ship without, so the memory makers' output sets the shipment ceiling.
rationale: Micron says its stacked-memory shipment growth is capped by supply rather than demand and directly gates NVIDIA and AMD availability, Morgan Stanley sees no sign of easing and flags worse shortages in 2027 and 2028, and one supplier's chief executive says constraints could run through 2027 while packaging capacity is visibly expanding.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to yields on the next stacked-memory generation now entering production.

falsifiableTrigger: Memory supplier grossMargin falls for two consecutive quarters as contract prices flatten.
mechanism: Memory suppliers set prices in a shortage, so more of the money paid for each AI server ends up with them rather than the system builder.
rationale: Micron's data-centre segment reported $11.5 billion of revenue, up 103% quarter over quarter, at an 87% gross margin, contract prices are locked in at high-teen to low-twenties percent increases with all 2026 output pre-allocated, and next-generation stacked-memory prices are forecast to roughly double into 2027.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to how fast new memory capacity arrives and breaks the pricing power.

falsifiableTrigger: No new sovereign or enterprise cluster above 10,000 GPUs is announced for two consecutive quarters.
mechanism: Governments and large companies are now placing orders big enough to sit alongside the cloud giants in the same allocation queue.
rationale: A Japanese national project will deploy 27,500 accelerators and 13,750 processors across 140 megawatts with the trade ministry, Firmus is building a 360-megawatt campus in Indonesia with up to 170,000 accelerators, a pharmaceutical company is installing eight of NVIDIA's newest systems, AMD launched a part aimed at sovereign and scientific buyers, and SK Group signed a partnership described as above $500 billion.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to public funding decisions, which can be cancelled faster than commercial contracts.

falsifiableTrigger: Intel data-center revenue growth falls below 10% year over year for two consecutive quarters.
mechanism: Growing server sales and a foundry that now wins outside customers give the market a third supplier of AI-adjacent capacity.
rationale: Intel's data-centre and AI revenue reached $6.3 billion, up 59% year over year with $2.5 billion of operating income, its foundry revenue reached $5.8 billion, up 31%, gross margin rose to 40.4% from 27.5%, it guided the next quarter above expectations, raised capital spending above $20 billion, and signed Fortinet as a named external foundry customer.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the newest production node holds its yield gains as volume rises.

falsifiableTrigger: New vendor equity-for-compute deals in marginalBuyerFinancing stop appearing for two consecutive quarters.
mechanism: Chip vendors now put their own money into the firms that buy their chips, so reported demand partly reflects vendor-funded customers.
rationale: AMD committed a strategic equity investment of up to $5 billion in Anthropic alongside its compute deal, NVIDIA invested an undisclosed amount in Safe Superintelligence alongside a platform commitment, and NVIDIA agreed to buy $5 billion of Intel stock tied to custom processor work.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether these customers can raise money from ordinary investors instead.

falsifiableTrigger: Standard DRAM S10 spot prices fall for two consecutive months as suppliers restore non-AI capacity.
mechanism: Memory makers move capacity to the highest-priced AI parts, which leaves less supply and higher prices for everything else.
rationale: AMD raised graphics bundle prices about 10% citing tight memory with graphics memory spot prices roughly tripled since late 2025, older standard memory hit $81.20 above its prior peak while the newer standard part broke $50 for the first time, suppliers are cutting output of older and embedded memory, and enterprise buyers now get priority on flash allocation over retail.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to when new fabrication capacity comes online and frees up older product lines.

falsifiableTrigger: No new multi-year accelerator-to-memory supply partnership is announced for two consecutive quarters through 2027.
mechanism: Accelerator makers sign directly with memory suppliers to reserve future output rather than compete for it later on the open market.
rationale: NVIDIA entered a long-term partnership with SK hynix to secure next-generation memory and jointly develop it, formalised inside a partnership with SK Group described as above $500 billion, and all three major memory makers have begun full-scale development of a 16-layer part specifically for NVIDIA targeting delivery by the fourth quarter of 2026.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether memory makers honour these reservations when spot prices run far above contract.

falsifiableTrigger: The leading supplier's HBM market-share-pct falls below 50% within four quarters as rivals ship volume.
mechanism: One supplier controls most of the memory every accelerator needs, so access to that single source decides who can build AI servers.
rationale: SK Hynix holds 56.4% of the stacked-memory market overall and about 62% of the next generation including roughly two-thirds of NVIDIA's supply, while Microsoft, Google and Meta have used cash reserves to lock long-term contracts that keep supply concentrated at the top tier.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the two rival memory makers reach volume on the next generation.

falsifiableTrigger: No new diversion prosecution or whitelist reduction is reported for two consecutive quarters.
mechanism: Prosecutions and a shorter approved-buyer list remove the intermediaries that moved restricted chips into China.
rationale: Taiwanese prosecutors expanded a criminal smuggling probe, raiding Supermicro's Taiwan office and affiliates and detaining employees over United States charges alleging some $2.5 billion of servers went to China without licences, and NVIDIA more than halved the list of Asian customers cleared to buy its chips.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether enforcement keeps up once licensed sales resume at scale.

falsifiableTrigger: CoWoS lead times stay above 52 weeks through the end of 2027 while the supply gap fails to narrow below 15%.
mechanism: Packaging capacity is being added faster than memory capacity, so the two constraints ease at different speeds and memory becomes the tighter one.
rationale: Both halves held: packaging capacity is ramping from about 80,000 toward 125,000 to 130,000 wafers a month with the supply gap narrowing from about 20% to about 10% by end-2026 and outside assembly partners adding more, yet lead times stay at 52 to 78 weeks with bookings into 2027 and TSMC says the gap runs through 2029 and 2030, while memory shows no easing at all.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether demand keeps growing fast enough to absorb the new packaging capacity as it lands.

falsifiableTrigger: NAND contract prices for server drives fall for two consecutive quarters while Rubin deployments keep growing.
mechanism: A new storage tier inside each rack multiplies the number of drives per system, which pulls flash demand up faster than supply can follow.
rationale: NVIDIA's newest generation adds a storage tier expected to pull flash demand from about 35 million terabytes this year to more than 100 million next year with each unit carrying 576 drives, enterprise contracts now get priority allocation over retail, and flash scarcity is already showing up in rack costs rising 2 to 3% a week.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to how quickly the newest generation actually deploys at volume.

falsifiableTrigger: Every major cloud provider publishes list rates for its newest rack-scale systems for 2 consecutive quarters.
mechanism: Providers differ in how they sell scarce new hardware, so some withhold list rates while others publish them, which makes public pricing an incomplete guide.
rationale: ADJUSTED: Some cloud providers now quote their newest rack systems only through sales while others still publish rates for the same class of hardware, so public price pages show only part of what leading-edge capacity costs.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to how scarce the newest systems are, since providers publish rates once supply is comfortable.

falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA accelerator market-share-pct stabilises or rises for 2 consecutive quarters while rival shipments grow.
mechanism: The whole market is growing faster than NVIDIA can supply it, so rivals absorb the extra growth without taking existing business away.
rationale: One projection has NVIDIA's accelerator share falling from a 2024 peak of 87% to 81% in 2025 and 75% in 2026, other estimates put it at about 70 to 80% and expect further erosion as custom chips grow 44.6% against 16.1% for merchant parts, yet its data-centre revenue set a record $75.2 billion, up 92% year over year.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether rival volume lands on schedule, since share estimates rest on forecasts rather than shipped units.

falsifiableTrigger: A major buyer returns to purchasing loose accelerators rather than vendor racks for a flagship cluster within 2 quarters.
mechanism: Vendors now ship complete racks with their own networking and software, so buyers compare finished systems instead of individual parts.
rationale: AMD launched its first production rack-scale system with 72 accelerators positioned directly against NVIDIA's 72-accelerator rack, NVIDIA's newest rack entered production ramp across the major clouds, and both vendors now compete on whole-rack claims such as tokens per dollar rather than on single chips.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to open rack standards that would let buyers assemble their own systems again.

falsifiableTrigger: Power transformer lead times fall below 80 weeks for 2 consecutive quarters.
mechanism: A new site cannot energise until its electrical gear arrives, so multi-year equipment waits set the schedule regardless of chip availability.
rationale: Power transformer lead times now average 128 weeks and reach 200 weeks for specialty units serving chip plants, with prices up 77% since 2019, while Gartner projects 40% of AI data centres will be power-constrained by 2027.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to how fast electrical equipment makers add manufacturing capacity.

falsifiableTrigger: Median newest-generation gpuSpotPrice falls while prior-generation rates rise for 2 consecutive months.
mechanism: Scarce new systems command the highest hourly rates while older systems spread across many providers and compete on price.
rationale: The newest rack part's median rental rose about 42% over the year to $18.77 an hour while the two prior parts rose only about 11%, which supports the premium shifting forward, but older-part quotes did not clearly fall, with medians between $2.97 and $3.85, a range from $0.93 to $14.90 across 48 providers, and prices reported up 24% from their November 2025 low.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to how much older capacity comes off long-term contracts and back onto the open market.

detail.falsifiableTrigger: Alternative packaging upstreamLeadTimes rise above 52 weeks, or no accelerator maker places advanced-packaging volume outside TSMC for 2 consecutive quarters.
detail.mechanism: Much shorter quoted waits at rival packaging houses give chip makers a way to add output without waiting in TSMC's booked queue.
detail.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the alternative suppliers can match the yield and quality that leading accelerators need.
detail.statement: Accelerator makers are starting to route advanced-packaging work to Samsung, Amkor, ASE and Intel because those suppliers quote far shorter waits than TSMC.
detail.title: Packaging work starts to spread beyond TSMC

detail.falsifiableTrigger: AMD's share of CoWoS output in pkgCapacityOrderSpread rises above 15% within 2 quarters.
detail.mechanism: One shared and scarce packaging allocation means AMD cannot grow both of its data-centre product lines at the same time.
detail.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether AMD can buy more packaging slots or move some work to other packaging houses.
detail.statement: AMD holds only about a tenth of TSMC's advanced-packaging output and must split it between its server processors and its accelerators, so every processor it packages costs it an accelerator.
detail.title: AMD's packaging slots force a product trade-off

falsifiableTrigger: B200 rpoBacklog falls below 2 million units for 2 consecutive quarters.
mechanism: Buyers commit to accelerator orders years before delivery, so the order book keeps growing faster than NVIDIA can build and ship systems.
rationale: NVIDIA posted record data-center revenue of $75.2 billion, up 92 percent year over year, and guided the next quarter to $91 billion, while the order book kept growing: a B200 backlog of about 3.6 million units, purchase orders in hand from almost all major customers ahead of the Vera Rubin ramp, and more than $750 billion of infrastructure agreements under negotiation. Vera Rubin racks entered production ramp across several clouds and server suppliers report an order boom spilling into the second half of 2026, so demand still runs ahead of what NVIDIA can deliver.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to a large buyer cancelling or deferring committed orders, which would show the order book shrinking while shipments keep rising.

falsifiableTrigger: HBM leadTimes ease to available-on-demand and CoWoS lead times fall below 26 weeks before the end of 2027.
mechanism: Every accelerator needs both stacked memory and advanced packaging, so whichever is scarcer sets the ceiling on how many units vendors can ship.
rationale: Both limits held this cycle and one got sharper. Advanced packaging is booked at 52 to 78 week waits with lines full through 2027, while stacked memory is sold out for 2026 and much of 2027, with one bank saying it sees no sign of easing and flagging worse shortages in 2027 and 2028. The strongest new point is that NVIDIA reportedly cut the memory in its next flagship part from 288 gigabytes to 192 gigabytes because it cannot get enough supply, which is a shortage changing the product itself.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to memory capacity additions landing sooner than the announced late-2026 and 2027 dates.

falsifiableTrigger: AMD accelerator market-share-pct fails to rise above 7% through 2027.
mechanism: Buyers short of NVIDIA supply will qualify a second rack vendor, so AMD's production racks and named gigawatt commitments convert into shipped share.
rationale: AMD put its Helios rack into production with shipments starting in the third quarter of 2026, launched the MI455X, and named Anthropic at up to 2 gigawatts, OpenAI at 6 gigawatts, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle. Its data-center segment grew 57 percent year over year to $5.8 billion in the first quarter and analysts see data-center GPU revenue roughly doubling this year. The caveats are real: AMD still holds only about 5 to 7 percent of the accelerator market, its second-quarter results are not yet published, and one supply-chain account puts the true volume ramp at the second quarter of 2027, so this is share conversion in progress rather than proven.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the Helios ramp holds its second-half-2026 schedule rather than slipping to 2027.

falsifiableTrigger: ASIC market-share-pct growth falls back below GPU growth for 2 consecutive quarters.
mechanism: Large cloud buyers move their steady inference work onto chips they design themselves, which takes growth that would otherwise go to merchant GPUs.
rationale: Forecasts now put custom-chip growth at 44.6 percent for 2026 against 16.1 percent for merchant GPUs, with custom parts at 27.8 percent of AI servers and overtaking GPU shipments by 2028. Hyperscaler custom silicon spending is projected to more than triple from $8 billion in 2024 to over $25 billion in 2026, Meta's four new in-house accelerators enter production in September 2026, Broadcom carries a $73 billion AI backlog, and Google has committed to more than 3 million units of Intel packaging for its next chip. Against that, GPUs still make up about 60 percent of one large cloud's build.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether in-house parts actually reach volume production on schedule rather than staying captive pilots.

falsifiableTrigger: gpuSpotPrice for H100 or GB200 drops more than 20% within a quarter.
mechanism: Scarce accelerators let owners hold their rental rates because renters have nowhere cheaper to go for current-generation capacity.
rationale: Rental levels held rather than improved. CoreWeave still lists its single-GPU instance at $6.50 per GPU-hour and publishes rack rates including a top-end system at $68.80 per hour for eight accelerators, while NVIDIA held a 75 percent gross margin and guided the next quarter to the same level. A marketplace snapshot shows older parts renting at $1.50 to $2.27 an hour with community hosts lower, so prices are firm at the top and soft at the bottom rather than broadly rising.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to a wave of new rack supply arriving faster than renters can absorb it.

falsifiableTrigger: exportControlExposure eases so China DC revenue recovers above prior levels within 2 quarters.
mechanism: Government licensing rules bar the best parts from the largest non-US market, so a block of willing buyers cannot legally be served.
rationale: NVIDIA's China revenue fell to $4,550 million from $9,659 million a year earlier, it recorded no Hopper data-center shipments to China, licences granted from February 2026 have produced no revenue, and the company assumes no China data-center revenue at all in its outlook. NVIDIA also more than halved the number of Asian customers cleared to buy its chips under a new compliance list, and AMD took about $440 million of charges from its own China restrictions.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to a policy change that clears the current top-end parts rather than only the cut-down ones.

falsifiableTrigger: Vendor-financed GPU commitments in rpoBacklog exceed 300,000 units within 2 quarters.
mechanism: When the seller guarantees the buyer's purchase, reported demand partly reflects the seller's own credit rather than independent budgets.
rationale: The vendor-financing programme grew from a pilot into a scaled business. NVIDIA now backstops purchases and rents back idle capacity for about 210,000 accelerators across two partners, after earlier support deals with CoreWeave and Lambda, funded by $25 billion of bonds raised in June. On top of that sit a discussed $350 billion facility for one model lab's chip purchases, up to $250 billion of backstop for its data-center leases, and an undisclosed equity investment in another lab that just committed to NVIDIA's next platform. Reporting explicitly flags that this concentrates demand in vendor-financed customers.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the backed customers can refinance on their own once the guarantees roll off.

falsifiableTrigger: customerConcentration for the top three direct customers falls below prior shares next fiscal year.
mechanism: A handful of buyers place most of the orders, so one of them slowing down removes a large slice of revenue at once.
rationale: The concentration figures are the same filings as before rather than a fresh quarter: three direct customers at 21, 17 and 16 percent of revenue, and in the prior fiscal year one customer at 22 percent with the four largest above half of revenue. What is new is the direction of travel, with commentary noting that the backstop and revenue-share arrangements may concentrate demand further in a small set of vendor-financed clouds.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether sovereign and enterprise orders grow fast enough to dilute the top few buyers.

falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA DC Ethernet switch market-share-pct slips from #1 within 2 quarters.
mechanism: Selling the switches and cabling with the accelerators makes the whole cluster one vendor's design, which raises the cost of swapping in someone else's chips.
rationale: NVIDIA became the revenue leader in data-center Ethernet switching for the first time in the first quarter of 2026 on networking bundled with its accelerators, and it named CoreWeave, Microsoft, Nebius, SpaceXAI and Tesla among the first customers for its newest switch generation. It also claims five times better network power efficiency across deployments above 100,000 accelerators and signed a long-term partnership to expand US optical manufacturing tenfold. Still, no finding compares networking growth against compute growth, so the narrower claim stands.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to buyers standardising on open rack and networking designs that let them mix vendors.

falsifiableTrigger: Cost-per-token gains stall so tokenEconomics improves less than one generation cycle.
mechanism: Each drop in the cost of serving a token makes more applications affordable, so cheaper compute brings in more work rather than less spending.
rationale: One cloud's new Rubin-based instance is quoted at ten times lower inference cost per token than the prior generation and one tenth the cost per million tokens versus the previous rack, NVIDIA says its current rack already cut cost per token by an order of magnitude, and open-model inference costs have fallen 30 to 50 percent a year since 2023. Usage is scaling alongside: one large enterprise is described as consuming roughly a trillion tokens a month.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether cheaper serving actually converts into paid usage rather than just lower bills.

falsifiableTrigger: Prepaid HBM commitments in rpoBacklog shrink or deposits are refunded within a quarter.
mechanism: Buyers who put cash down years ahead for memory they cannot cancel have already decided to build the accelerators that memory goes into.
rationale: Micron has signed 16 non-cancelable five-year take-or-pay agreements backed by more than $22 billion of cash and related commitments, including nearly $18 billion of deposits. All three memory makers have their 2026 output pre-allocated under locked contracts, order books now extend into 2028, and NVIDIA signed a long-term supply and joint-development partnership with one supplier for its next memory generation.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether any deposit-backed contract is renegotiated or written down.

falsifiableTrigger: exportControlExposure changes lift the sub-50% China cap or clear Blackwell within 2 quarters.
mechanism: Licences let a limited set of buyers order cut-down parts, but the volume cap, tariff and security conditions keep actual shipments near zero.
rationale: The picture the thesis described is now confirmed on both sides. Three sources restate the January 2026 rule change from denial to case-by-case review for the cut-down parts, with security conditions, a roughly 25 percent tariff and a cap of under half of comparable US sales. About $10 billion of licences are approved across roughly ten Chinese firms and first shipments have begun, but volumes are described as trivial, the top-end parts remain banned, and licences granted since February have produced no revenue.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the cap is raised or the current top-end parts are cleared for sale.

falsifiableTrigger: Memory hbmSupplyCapex expansion pulls DRAM/NVMe prices down within 2 quarters.
mechanism: Memory and drives are a large slice of a server's parts cost, so their price rises land straight on the bill for every rack built.
rationale: Rack component costs are running up about 2 to 3 percent a week and sit 10 to 15 percent above baseline on memory and drive scarcity. Server memory contract prices are forecast up more than 25 percent quarter over quarter, server memory up 18 percent in the third quarter, one supplier is seeking up to a 20 percent increase with quotes valid for only 72 hours, memory component waits have stretched to 32 to 40-plus weeks with prices up about 90 percent since late 2025, and next-generation stacked memory contract prices are forecast to roughly double into 2027.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to new memory fabrication capacity coming online and easing contract prices.

falsifiableTrigger: releaseCadence slips push a major vendor's 2H-2026 ramp into 2027.
mechanism: Each vendor's ramp is gated by its own packaging and memory allocation, so production start dates cluster while shipped volume does not.
rationale: The staged reading held up in detail. NVIDIA's newest rack entered production ramp in the third quarter of 2026, AMD's rack reached full production with third-quarter shipment start but ramps into the second half of 2027, its largest named customer takes its first gigawatt only in the first half of 2027, and one supply-chain account still puts AMD's mass production at the second quarter of 2027. Meta's in-house parts enter production in September 2026. So several vendors are producing at once, but their volumes arrive at different times.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to further manufacturing delays at the challenger vendors, which would stretch the wave out further.

falsifiableTrigger: AMD customerConcentration eases as its buyer base broadens over the next 2 quarters.
mechanism: A few very large commitments make up most of the growth, so one of them slipping moves the whole forecast.
rationale: AMD's announced accelerator commitments sit with a handful of names: 6 gigawatts each at two customers, up to 2 gigawatts at a third, plus a July expansion at a fourth. AMD's own filings say it depends on a small number of customers for a substantial share of business and expects that to continue. Its own product launch disclosed no order quantities or revenue guidance, so the mega-deals carry the story.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether mid-size and enterprise buyers start placing orders large enough to matter.

falsifiableTrigger: Crescent Island releaseCadence slips its customer sampling past the 2H 2026 quarter.
mechanism: Using ordinary memory instead of stacked memory lets a chip skip the two scarcest steps in the supply chain, so it can be built when others cannot.
rationale: The plan is unchanged and still unproven. Intel's inference part uses standard low-power memory rather than stacked memory specifically to avoid the packaging and stacked-memory squeeze, and is still guided to customer sampling in the second half of 2026. Two sources disagree on the memory size, quoting 160 gigabytes and up to 480 gigabytes, and neither reports a customer, an order or a shipment.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the part samples on time and wins a named customer rather than staying a demonstration.

falsifiableTrigger: TSMC grossMargin declines for 2 consecutive quarters as capacity loosens.
mechanism: When demand for chips of every kind fills the factories, the foundry can pick the most profitable orders and charge more for them.
rationale: TSMC reported a 67.7 percent gross margin, up 9.1 points year over year, revenue up 36 percent, and raised its full-year growth guidance from over 30 percent to more than 40 percent on AI-server and high-performance computing demand. It says packaging capacity is so tight it is limiting customer growth with the gap running through 2029-2030, it lifted 2026 capital spending by about $10 billion to $60-64 billion, and it added a further $100 billion US commitment.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to capacity additions arriving faster than orders, which would end the ability to raise prices.

falsifiableTrigger: A hyperscalerCapexRevision cuts 2026 or 2027 AI capex guidance within 2 quarters.
mechanism: Cloud buyers fund accelerators years before the revenue arrives, so a disappointing payback would force them to cut orders quickly.
rationale: The spending jump got bigger and the market started to push back. The four largest US cloud buyers plan about $725 billion of 2026 capital spending, up roughly 77 percent, with one raising guidance twice this year to $195-205 billion and promising another rise in 2027, and one neocloud roughly doubling its own budget to $31-35 billion. On the same earnings day that buyer's shares fell about 6 percent and other AI-linked names fell with it, chip stocks fell in mid-July on spending jitters, and analysts warned the capex jump may be unsustainable. No buyer has actually cut guidance, so this stays a risk rather than an event.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to cloud revenue growth keeping pace with the spending, which so far it has.

falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA grossMargin guidance drops below 70% in a coming quarter.
mechanism: Buyers with no ready alternative pay the asking price, so the vendor keeps a high margin even while absorbing the cost of a new product ramp.
rationale: The evidence is the same quarter as before rather than a new one: a 75.0 percent gross margin with the next quarter guided to the same level. The gap to rivals is still wide, with AMD at 55 percent guiding to about 56 percent and Intel at 40.4 percent, but Intel's margin rose 12.9 points year over year, so the gap is narrowing from below even as NVIDIA holds its level.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to memory and packaging cost rises that the vendor cannot pass on.

falsifiableTrigger: Top-buyer customerConcentration in CoWoS output falls below 85% within a year.
mechanism: A few buyers hold nearly all the packaging slots, so if one stops ordering there is no queue of other customers able to take that volume.
rationale: Three sources now put the top three packaging customers above 85 percent of output, with the largest at roughly 60 percent and about 595,000 wafers, and the second at about 11 percent. One adds that capacity is pre-booked above 85 percent for both 2026 and 2027, and that the largest buyer has booked more than half of the coming expansion, so the concentration extends into future capacity rather than just today's.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to smaller accelerator designers winning enough volume to spread the bookings.

falsifiableTrigger: Aggregate rpoBacklog duration shortens as new commitments turn shorter-dated over 2 quarters.
mechanism: Buyers worried about getting capacity at all sign longer contracts, which pushes the average delivery date of the order book further into the future.
rationale: One cloud's backlog rose more than $50 billion in a quarter to $514 billion with only just over half expected to convert within 24 months, which means the rest is booked further out. A neocloud's contracted backlog reached $99.4 billion and it holds a purchase commitment running through 2032, memory makers have signed five-year non-cancelable contracts with order books into 2028, and a $500-billion-plus infrastructure partnership targets its first site in 2027.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to supply loosening, which would let buyers go back to shorter contracts.

falsifiableTrigger: A leading model provider reports revenue (apiArr) growth stalling quarter over quarter while compute commitments keep growing.
mechanism: Model providers pay for compute out of subscription and usage revenue, so rising sales make their multi-year compute commitments fundable.
rationale: Only one revenue datapoint appears this cycle: one leading model provider at more than $30 billion of annualised revenue as of April 2026, up from $1 billion in January 2025. Its own compute chief says access to compute is central to keeping its model at the frontier, and an enterprise customer is described as consuming roughly a trillion tokens a month, which is usage rather than provider revenue. That is consistent with the thesis but adds no new proof.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the largest labs still fund compute from sales rather than from vendor equity and credit.

falsifiableTrigger: Chinese domestic accelerator designWins for frontier training stall over the next 2 quarters.
mechanism: With the best foreign chips barred, Chinese buyers fund local designs, and each successful large training run makes the local option more credible.
rationale: The capability side is now corroborated twice: a 1.6-trillion-parameter model pretrained entirely on more than 50,000 domestic accelerators across over 35 trillion tokens. New this cycle, domestic vendors are also scaling commercially, with one guiding first-half revenue up 135 to 149 percent and another up 56 to 70 percent. The volume gap still stands, with Chinese firms ordering more than two million restricted NVIDIA parts against roughly 700,000 units of inventory, and in-house chips at two Chinese labs judged more than two years away.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether domestic supply can be produced in volume, given the memory and software limits the sources acknowledge.

falsifiableTrigger: A neocloud's marginalBuyerFinancing debt load or net loss narrows for 2 consecutive quarters.
mechanism: Buying accelerators on borrowed money creates depreciation and interest immediately while the rental revenue arrives over years.
rationale: The same pattern with no new quarter: revenue up about 168 percent from $1.9 billion to $5.1 billion while the net loss widened from $937 million to $1.2 billion. Debt rose 16.1 percent in one quarter to $24.86 billion, and the company roughly doubled its capital spending plan to $31-35 billion, so the spending that drives the losses is still increasing.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to rental rates holding long enough for the fleets to pay back their cost.

falsifiableTrigger: A top hyperscaler cuts its 2027 gigawatt power target below its 2026 level.
mechanism: A site can only run as many accelerators as its electricity supply allows, so power decides how much hardware can actually be switched on.
rationale: Buildouts are now quoted in gigawatts almost everywhere: one buyer plans 7 gigawatts of compute in 2026 and roughly double in 2027, accelerator commitments are stated as 6, 6 and 2 gigawatts, a Korean cloud is sized at 2 gigawatts, a partnership covers 2-plus gigawatts of data centres, and a Japanese site is described by its 140 megawatts. The sharpest new evidence is that NVIDIA's next flagship reportedly had its memory cut partly because of data-centre power limits, with chip-level power around 1,800 watts and up to 2,600 to 2,800 watts for a higher variant.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to efficiency gains, which let the same power run more work each generation.

falsifiableTrigger: Broadcom-plus-Marvell market-share-pct of custom ASIC co-design falls below 90% within a year.
mechanism: Cloud buyers lack the in-house engineering to take a chip from design to production, so they hand that work to the same two outside firms.
rationale: The concentration figure is restated by one source at an estimated 95 percent of custom AI chip co-design held by two firms, and one of them carries a $73 billion backlog. Two early counter-signals appeared: one model lab is in early-stage talks with Samsung to build a custom chip on a 2 nanometre process, and one cloud committed to more than 3 million units of Intel packaging for its next in-house chip with delivery in 2028. Neither is a co-design win yet, so the dependence stands but the edges are starting to fray.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the early Samsung and Intel engagements turn into shipped custom parts.

falsifiableTrigger: Wistron odmMonthlyAiRevenue falls year-over-year for 2 consecutive months.
mechanism: Contract makers only book revenue when finished systems leave the factory, so their monthly sales track actual shipments rather than orders.
rationale: One contract maker posted record June revenue of NT$321.82 billion, up 53.9 percent year over year and 10.9 percent month over month, on AI-server and networking shipments, and opened a 324,000-square-foot plant in Texas to build AI systems. Server supply-chain players report an order boom spilling into the second half of 2026. That is one month from one maker, consistent with the thesis but not more proof than before.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to component shortages stalling assembly even while orders stay strong.

falsifiableTrigger: A neocloud's marginalBuyerFinancing debt-to-equity rises above 6:1 within 2 quarters.
mechanism: Accelerator fleets are bought with borrowed money against contracted rental income, so the equity cushion stays thin as the fleet grows.
rationale: One neocloud has raised $18.81 billion of debt against $3.5 billion of equity, a 5.4 to 1 ratio, with total debt of $24.86 billion up 16.1 percent in a single quarter, while its net loss widened to $1.2 billion. Separately, NVIDIA is backstopping purchases and agreeing to rent back idle capacity for smaller clouds, which is a sign these buyers cannot carry the risk on their own balance sheets.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to credit conditions, since refinancing at higher rates would strain the model quickly.

falsifiableTrigger: Co-packaged optics adoption stalls below 5% of AI optical modules through 2027.
mechanism: Putting the optics into the switch package cuts the power and parts needed to wire a cluster, which moves cluster supply onto the optics roadmap.
rationale: The adoption path is now quantified: co-packaged optics goes from about 0.5 percent of AI optical modules in 2026 to about 35 percent by 2030, with one vendor's photonics switch due in the second half of 2026 and another shipping early in 2026. Taiwanese packaging houses are newly competing for silicon photonics work as data-centre architectures upgrade, one vendor claims five times better network power efficiency from photonics, and NVIDIA signed a long-term partnership to raise US optical connectivity capacity tenfold across three new plants.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to manufacturing yields on packaged optics, which decide whether the ramp curve holds.

falsifiableTrigger: A named US fab or packaging project slips its build milestone past 2027.
mechanism: Trade policy and customer pressure push each step of AI hardware into US plants, which adds capacity that does not depend on Taiwan.
rationale: The commitments now span the whole chain, not just assembly. NVIDIA plans up to $500 billion of US-built AI infrastructure with named partners, a contract maker opened a Texas plant for its systems, an optics partnership adds three US plants and more than 3,000 jobs, a memory maker committed $250 billion through 2035 targeting 40 percent domestic output and broke ground on a New York fab in July, the leading foundry added a further $100 billion US investment, and Intel raised capital spending above $20 billion while ramping its newest node.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether these announcements convert into working capacity on schedule rather than staying pledges.

falsifiableTrigger: Google Cloud or CoreWeave rpoBacklog fails to grow sequentially for 2 consecutive quarters.
mechanism: Clouds sign compute contracts faster than they can install capacity, so the unfilled order book shows demand earlier than reported sales do.
rationale: One cloud's backlog rose more than $50 billion sequentially to $514 billion from $462 billion, with just over half expected to convert within 24 months, while its revenue accelerated 82 percent year over year to $24.8 billion and its operating income more than tripled to $8.8 billion. A neocloud's contracted backlog reached $99.4 billion from $66.8 billion a month earlier. Both bookings and delivered revenue are rising, with bookings rising faster.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to how much of the backlog is from a few very large customers whose plans could change.

falsifiableTrigger: A top hyperscaler returns to positive free cash flow while holding 2027 capex guidance for 2 consecutive quarters.
mechanism: Capital spending has outgrown the cash the businesses generate, so buyers cover the gap by issuing debt and shares.
rationale: The clearest evidence yet: one of the largest cloud buyers funded its quarter's build with $49.6 billion of equity issuance and $20.3 billion of senior unsecured notes, and reported its first-ever negative free cash flow of $5.9 billion, while raising 2026 spending guidance for the second time this year. A neocloud's debt rose 16.1 percent in a quarter to $24.86 billion, and even NVIDIA raised $25 billion of bonds to fund customer purchases.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to borrowing costs and investor appetite, which decide how long this can continue.

falsifiableTrigger: A new accelerator generation delivers less than a 1.5x perfPerWatt gain over its predecessor.
mechanism: Each generation does more work for the same electricity and the same packaging slot, so buyers get more capacity without more of the scarce inputs.
rationale: Two separate announcements put the newest rack at ten times the work per megawatt of what it replaces, a switch line claims five times better network power efficiency across deployments above 100,000 accelerators, and a memory maker claims 2.5 times better performance per watt on its newest flash. An independent measure of the prior step was a more modest 1.6 times. Against that, the next flagship chip is reported at roughly 1,800 watts, so per-chip power is climbing even as work per watt improves.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to vendor-claimed efficiency figures, since the one independent measurement is far smaller than the marketing numbers.

falsifiableTrigger: HBM leadTimes shorten and suppliers report unsold capacity for 2 consecutive quarters before end-2027.
mechanism: Every accelerator needs a fixed amount of stacked memory, so when memory runs short vendors must ship fewer units or put less memory on each one.
rationale: This is the cycle's strongest evidence. NVIDIA reportedly cut its next flagship's memory from 288 gigabytes in a 12-high stack to 192 gigabytes in an 8-high stack, driven mainly by memory supply limits, which is scarcity redesigning the product. Around that, stacked memory is sold out for 2026 with much of 2027 pre-booked, one bank sees no sign of easing and flags worse shortages in 2027 and 2028, a supplier chief says constraints could persist through 2027, another supplier says conditions stay tight beyond 2027 with order books into 2028, and memory component waits have stretched to 32 to 40-plus weeks on allocation only.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to the announced capacity expansions, including a 50 percent capacity increase at one supplier, arriving on schedule.

falsifiableTrigger: Memory supplier grossMargin falls for 2 consecutive quarters as contract prices flatten.
mechanism: Memory is the scarcest part in the rack, so its suppliers set the price and take a bigger share of what the finished server earns.
rationale: One memory maker's data-centre segment reported $11.5 billion of revenue, up 103 percent quarter over quarter, at an 87 percent gross margin, which is far above any chip or system vendor in this corpus. Contract prices support it: server memory forecast up more than 25 percent quarter over quarter, one supplier seeking up to a 20 percent increase, contracts locked in at high-teen to low-twenties percent rises, and next-generation stacked memory prices forecast to roughly double into 2027.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to new memory capacity arriving and breaking the pricing power.

falsifiableTrigger: No new sovereign or enterprise cluster above 10,000 GPUs is announced for 2 consecutive quarters.
mechanism: Governments and large firms now buy their own clusters instead of renting, which adds a buyer group that does not follow cloud spending cycles.
rationale: Government-linked and enterprise orders got much larger. A Japanese national project takes 27,500 accelerators and 13,750 processors across 140 megawatts developed with the trade ministry, a Korean telecom will build a 2-gigawatt AI cloud, and a Korean group partnership is described as $500 billion-plus with the first site in 2027. On the enterprise side a pharmaceutical firm is deploying eight of the newest systems as a second cluster, AMD launched a part aimed specifically at sovereign and scientific buyers, and named a telecom and a networking firm as adopters.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether announced national projects are funded and built rather than signed as letters of intent.

falsifiableTrigger: Intel data-center revenue growth falls below 10% year over year for 2 consecutive quarters.
mechanism: Better factory yields and a filling order book let Intel sell more server parts and outside manufacturing at improving margins.
rationale: Intel's data-centre and AI revenue reached $6.3 billion in the second quarter, up 59 percent year over year with $2.5 billion of operating income, gross margin rose to 40.4 percent from 27.5 percent, foundry revenue reached $5.8 billion up 31 percent with narrowing losses, and third-quarter guidance came in above expectations. It also won its first external foundry customer, took a commitment for more than 3 million units of its packaging for a cloud's next in-house chip, and is adding capacity in Ireland and beyond $20 billion of capital spending.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the newest process node holds its yield as volume rises.

falsifiableTrigger: New vendor equity-for-compute deals in marginalBuyerFinancing stop appearing for 2 consecutive quarters.
mechanism: A vendor that owns part of its customer helps fund the purchase of its own chips, so some reported demand is money the vendor supplied.
rationale: AMD committed a strategic equity investment of up to $5 billion in the model lab that agreed to take up to 2 gigawatts of its accelerators, confirmed by two of its own disclosures. NVIDIA made an undisclosed investment in another lab alongside that lab's commitment to its next platform, holds $5 billion of Intel stock tied to custom processors for its platforms, and offers startups compute in exchange for a share of future revenue. So the practice now spans both merchant vendors.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the funded customers can raise money independently once the vendor stops writing cheques.

falsifiableTrigger: Standard DRAM S10 spot prices fall for 2 consecutive months as suppliers restore non-AI capacity.
mechanism: Suppliers shift wafers to the highest-priced AI memory, which starves the ordinary parts used in consumer and general-purpose products.
rationale: Older standard memory hit $81.20 for a 16-gigabyte part, up 17.5 percent in a month and above its prior peak, while the newer standard part broke $50 for the first time after sitting at $39 to $41 in the spring. Suppliers are cutting older and embedded output to prioritise higher-margin parts, with new capacity not online until late 2026. AMD is raising graphics card bundle prices about 10 percent citing tight memory, with graphics memory spot prices roughly tripled since late 2025, and consumer drives are being squeezed as enterprise contracts get priority.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to new fabrication capacity coming online in late 2026 and freeing standard output.

falsifiableTrigger: No new multi-year accelerator-to-memory supply partnership is announced for 2 consecutive quarters through 2027.
mechanism: With memory the scarcest input, accelerator makers contract directly with suppliers and co-develop the parts so their allocation is locked before rivals bid.
rationale: NVIDIA entered a long-term partnership with one memory maker to secure next-generation supply and jointly develop stacked memory, inside a $500-billion-plus group partnership that explicitly covers memory supply. All three memory makers have begun full-scale development of 16-high next-generation stacks specifically for NVIDIA, targeting delivery by the end of 2026, and one Korean AI cloud is specified with that supplier's memory. Memory makers have separately signed multi-year non-cancelable contracts backed by deposits.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to memory supply loosening, which would remove the reason to pre-commit.

falsifiableTrigger: The leading supplier's HBM market-share-pct falls below 50% within 4 quarters as rivals ship volume.
mechanism: One supplier holds most of the qualified stacked-memory output, so its allocation decisions set who can build accelerators.
rationale: The lead is confirmed at 56.4 percent of the stacked-memory market, and about 62 percent of the next generation with roughly two thirds of NVIDIA's supply, restated by a second source. The largest cloud buyers have used cash reserves to lock long-term contracts, keeping access concentrated at the top. Two facts cut the other way: all three makers are now in full-scale development of the newest stack for NVIDIA, and one rival is reported to be raising capacity 50 percent this year, so the lead may narrow.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the two rival suppliers qualify their newest stacks in volume.

falsifiableTrigger: No new diversion prosecution or whitelist reduction is reported for 2 consecutive quarters.
mechanism: Prosecuting resellers and shrinking the approved buyer list removes the intermediaries that moved restricted chips into China.
rationale: Taiwanese prosecutors expanded a criminal smuggling probe, raiding a server maker's Taiwan office and affiliates and detaining employees, tied to US charges alleging about $2.5 billion of servers were shipped to China without a licence. Separately NVIDIA more than halved the number of Asian customers authorised to buy its AI chips under a new compliance list, so both the prosecution and the whitelist sides tightened in the same cycle.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether new intermediaries appear faster than enforcement closes the old ones.

falsifiableTrigger: CoWoS lead times stay above 52 weeks through the end of 2027 while the supply gap fails to narrow below 15%.
mechanism: Packaging capacity can be added by building more lines within a year or two, while memory capacity takes longer and is being consumed faster, so the two limits ease at different speeds.
rationale: Both halves got firmer. On packaging, the shortfall is now put at about 10 percent in mid-2026, narrowed from about 20 percent in late 2025, against capacity of roughly 120,000 to 140,000 wafers a month and industry capacity approaching 200,000 including outside partners, yet waits stay at 52 to 78 weeks with lines booked through 2027 and the foundry now developing a rival packaging technique with a partner. On memory, one bank sees no sign of easing and flags worse shortages in 2027 and 2028, a supplier says tightness runs beyond 2027, and NVIDIA reportedly cut its next flagship's memory because supply is short.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the packaging gap keeps narrowing while order waits stay long, which would mean the easing is only on paper.

falsifiableTrigger: NAND contract prices for server drives fall for 2 consecutive quarters while Rubin deployments keep growing.
mechanism: The newest racks add a large drive tier next to the accelerators, so each rack shipped pulls in far more flash than the previous generation did.
rationale: Two sources put flash demand from the newest generation's memory tier rising from about 35 million terabytes this year to more than 100 million next year, with each unit carrying 576 drives for 9,600 terabytes, described as adding demand the size of a major phone maker. Enterprise contracts already get priority allocation over retail, rack component costs are running up 2 to 3 percent a week on memory and drive scarcity, and the industry has published a first standard for a new high-bandwidth flash tier.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to how quickly the newest racks actually deploy, since the demand forecast assumes a fast ramp.

falsifiableTrigger: Every major cloud provider publishes list rates for its newest rack-scale systems for 2 consecutive quarters.
mechanism: Providers move their scarcest new systems to negotiated contracts, so published price pages stop covering the leading-edge capacity.
rationale: The split the thesis describes is now visible side by side. One provider's public pricing page carries no rates for the newer parts and quotes longer terms only as custom pricing, and its on-demand catalogue lists no newer part and no AMD instances at all. Another provider does publish rates for the same class of hardware, including its newest rack system at $42.00 an hour and a top-end node at $68.80. A marketplace snapshot shows the newest part quoted only in a wide $6 to $12 range.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to supply loosening, which would push providers back to advertising list rates to fill capacity.

falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA accelerator market-share-pct stabilises or rises for 2 consecutive quarters while rival shipments grow.
mechanism: The market is growing faster than NVIDIA can supply it, so rivals absorb the extra growth and NVIDIA's percentage falls while its sales rise.
rationale: Three sources now put NVIDIA's accelerator share below its peak: a projected fall from 87 percent in 2024 to 81 percent in 2025 and 75 percent in 2026, about 70 percent in another estimate, and roughly 70 to 80 percent in a third. Over the same period its data-centre revenue set a record at $75.2 billion, up 92 percent year over year, with the next quarter guided to $91 billion. One frequently quoted 90 percent figure is desktop add-in-board share and is explicitly not data-centre share.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to the share numbers being projections from analysts rather than measured shipments.

falsifiableTrigger: A major buyer returns to purchasing loose accelerators rather than vendor racks for a flagship cluster within 2 quarters.
mechanism: Performance now depends on how the whole rack is wired and cooled, so vendors sell finished racks and buyers compare complete systems.
rationale: AMD launched a 72-accelerator rack with 31 terabytes of stacked memory and 2.9 exaFLOPS per rack, positioned directly against NVIDIA's 72-accelerator rack, reached full production with third-quarter shipments, and named five large adopters. It sells the rack with its own processors, networking and software, claiming 30 percent more tokens per dollar than the rival rack and software gains of 3.3 times on inference. NVIDIA's equivalent rack entered production ramp across several clouds in the same window.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to open rack standards, which would let buyers mix parts from different vendors again.

falsifiableTrigger: Power transformer lead times fall below 80 weeks for 2 consecutive quarters.
mechanism: Heavy electrical gear is built to order with multi-year queues, so a site cannot energise until its equipment arrives regardless of chip supply.
note: grid-equipment-lead-times-gate-new-ai-sites: applied: corroborated secondary reversal (5 distinct publishers; pending filing checkpoint)
rationale: No finding in this cycle reports transformer or grid equipment lead times at all, so the specific claim has no fresh support. The delivery constraints that sources do name are memory, at 32 to 40-plus weeks and with no sign of easing, and packaging at 52 to 78 weeks. Power still appears, but as the unit buyers size their plans in and as a chip-level design limit, not as an equipment delivery queue, so the thesis holds less weight than the constraints being measured.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether any source measures grid equipment waits at all, since none did this cycle.

falsifiableTrigger: Median newest-generation gpuSpotPrice falls while prior-generation rates rise for 2 consecutive months.
mechanism: Scarce new systems command a premium while older parts compete on price across many owners, so the spread widens by generation.
rationale: One snapshot shows the price ladder the thesis expects: the older part at roughly $1.50 to $2.27 an hour on verified datacentre hosts and $0.90 to $1.60 on community hosts, the middle part at $3.50 to $5.50, and the newest at roughly $6 to $12. A provider list shows the same stepping, with a newer node at $68.80 an hour against $49.24 for the older one. This is a single point in time, so it shows a spread by generation but not the movement over time the thesis claims.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to having repeated price snapshots over time, since a single reading cannot show a trend.

falsifiableTrigger: Alternative packaging upstreamLeadTimes rise above 52 weeks, or no accelerator maker places advanced-packaging volume outside TSMC for 2 consecutive quarters.
mechanism: Rival packaging houses quote roughly half the wait, so buyers stuck in the queue move work to them to get parts sooner.
rationale: This moved from being considered to being ordered. One cloud has committed to more than 3 million units of Intel's packaging for its next in-house chip with delivery in 2028, and TSMC responded by announcing development of a competing technique with a partner in late July. Alternative routes at Samsung and one assembly house are quoted at 26 to 39 weeks against 52 to 78 at TSMC, NVIDIA is reported to be weighing moving some next-generation output to Intel, two other assembly firms are adding capacity, and industry capacity including outside partners could approach 200,000 wafers a month.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether alternative packaging yields match TSMC's on the largest, hardest parts.

falsifiableTrigger: AMD's share of CoWoS output in pkgCapacityOrderSpread rises above 15% within 2 quarters.
mechanism: AMD's packaging allocation is fixed in the short run and shared across two product lines, so building more of one means building fewer of the other.
rationale: The claim rests on the same single source as before: AMD holds roughly 11 percent of the leading foundry's packaging output, about 105,000 wafers, and must split it between its server processors and its accelerators, so every processor slot used is not available for an accelerator. A second source corroborates the concentration picture and AMD's position outside the top buyer. No finding this cycle shows AMD's allocation changing or the trade-off being resolved.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to AMD securing packaging outside the leading foundry, which would remove the forced choice.

detail.falsifiableTrigger: The next flagship ships with its originally planned 288GB memory configuration within 2 quarters of launch.
detail.mechanism: When a vendor cannot buy enough memory or power for its planned design, it ships a smaller configuration rather than fewer machines.
detail.sensitivity: Most sensitive to this being a single report so far, and to memory supply improving before the part goes into volume production.
detail.statement: NVIDIA has reportedly cut the memory in its next flagship accelerator from 288 gigabytes to 192 gigabytes because it cannot secure enough stacked memory and because sites cannot supply enough power.
detail.title: Memory shortage now shrinks the product, not just the volume

detail.falsifiableTrigger: The first Korean AI factory misses its 2027 target or the partnership is not converted from letters of intent into signed contracts within 2 quarters.
detail.mechanism: Tying memory supply, construction and cloud capacity into one partnership gives both sides a reason to build the whole chain in the same country.
detail.sensitivity: Most sensitive to the deals still being letters of intent rather than binding orders.
detail.statement: NVIDIA and one Korean group have tied together data-centre construction, memory supply and cloud capacity in a partnership described as more than $500 billion, making Korea a second hub of the buildout alongside the United States.
detail.title: Korea becomes a second centre of the AI buildout

detail.falsifiableTrigger: No accelerator or system vendor announces a shipping product using the high-bandwidth flash specification within 4 quarters.
detail.mechanism: Flash is far cheaper and more plentiful than stacked memory, so moving part of the memory job onto drives relieves the scarcest input in the rack.
detail.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the speed grades in the specification are fast enough to replace stacked memory for real work.
detail.statement: The industry has published a first standard for a high-bandwidth flash tier and is designing racks around large drive pools, creating a cheaper memory layer that does not compete for scarce stacked-memory supply.
detail.title: Flash steps in where stacked memory runs out

detail.falsifiableTrigger: AMD software releases deliver less than a 1.5x measured inference gain over the prior release for 2 consecutive releases.
detail.mechanism: Software tuning raises the work a shipped accelerator does without needing new silicon, so it improves the value of AMD's installed hardware immediately.
detail.sensitivity: Most sensitive to these being vendor-reported figures on selected workloads rather than independent benchmarks.
detail.statement: AMD is reporting large software-driven speedups on its current accelerators, which lifts its competitiveness now even though its new racks do not ship in volume until 2027.
detail.title: AMD's software gains arrive ahead of its volume

falsifiableTrigger: B200 rpoBacklog falls below 2 million units for 2 consecutive quarters.
mechanism: Buyers order more accelerators than NVIDIA can build, so orders pile up ahead of shipments and sales keep setting records.
rationale: NVIDIA posted record data-center revenue of $75.2 billion, up 92% year over year, and guided the next quarter to $91.0 billion, while the B200 order book stood at about 3.6 million units and Chinese buyers alone ordered over two million restricted parts against roughly 700,000 units of inventory. NVIDIA is also negotiating more than $750 billion of potential infrastructure agreements, and SpaceX said it will build exclusively on NVIDIA and expects a very significant share of 2027 output.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to a cut in hyperscaler capital spending plans, which would shrink the order book faster than shipments could catch up.

falsifiableTrigger: HBM leadTimes ease to available-on-demand and CoWoS lead times fall below 26 weeks before the end of 2027.
mechanism: Vendors cannot ship an accelerator without both a packaging slot and stacked memory, so whichever is scarcer sets the shipment ceiling.
rationale: TSMC advanced packaging is sold out with 52 to 78 week lead times and bookings into 2027 even as capacity ramps toward 125,000 to 130,000 wafers a month, and packaging lines are reported booked through 2027. High-bandwidth memory is sold out for all of 2026 and much of 2027 under non-cancellable contracts, with Micron saying tightness runs beyond calendar 2027 and order books extending into 2028.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to how fast new packaging and memory plants start producing usable output rather than how much money is announced for them.

falsifiableTrigger: AMD accelerator market-share-pct fails to rise above 7% through 2027.
mechanism: Large buyers sign for AMD racks years ahead, but AMD only takes share once those racks ship in volume, so commitments lead reported share by several quarters.
rationale: ADJUSTED: AMD has won gigawatt-scale accelerator commitments from OpenAI at 6 gigawatts, Anthropic at up to 2 gigawatts, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle, launched the MI400 series and its Helios rack into production on July 23, and grew data-center revenue 57% to $5.8 billion, yet its accelerator share stays near 5 to 7 percent against NVIDIA at roughly 80 to 90 percent because Helios shipments only start in the third quarter of 2026 and ramp into the second half of 2027, with one supply-chain account putting first production output at the second quarter of 2027.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether Helios volume production slips from 2026 into late 2027, which would push any share gain out another year.

falsifiableTrigger: ASIC market-share-pct growth falls back below GPU growth for 2 consecutive quarters.
mechanism: Every inference workload a hyperscaler moves onto its own chip is a merchant GPU it does not buy, so custom silicon eats into the growth merchant vendors would otherwise capture.
rationale: Custom chips are projected to grow 44.6% in 2026 against 16.1% for merchant GPUs, reaching 27.8% of AI servers and passing GPU shipments by 2028, while hyperscaler custom silicon spend rises from $15 billion in 2025 to over $25 billion in 2026. Meta's four new in-house accelerators enter production in September 2026, Broadcom carries a $73 billion AI backlog targeting $100 billion by 2027, Google has ordered more than 3 million units of Intel packaging for its next chip, and Anthropic is in early talks with Samsung about its own part.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether custom parts can handle training as well as inference; today they remain captive to their creators and unavailable to rent.

falsifiableTrigger: gpuSpotPrice for H100 or GB200 drops more than 20% within a quarter.
mechanism: As more prior-generation capacity comes online and buyers move to newer racks, sellers cut published hourly rates on the older hardware to keep it busy.
note: pricing-power-persistence: applied: corroborated secondary reversal (4 distinct publishers; pending filing checkpoint)
rationale: Published rental rates for the prior generation have fallen: Lambda lists H100 at $3.99 per GPU-hour and RunPod at $2.99 on August 5, against prior-cycle readings of $6.50 and $6.69, and CoreWeave quotes an 8-GPU H100 instance at $49.24 on demand and $19.71 spot. Separate coverage tracks H100 rental rates dropping from $7 to $10 an hour at launch to about $2 to $4 by late 2025, though used H100 hardware prices have held in a $25,000 to $40,000 range since mid-2024.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to which hardware generation is being priced; the newest systems are quoted only through sales, so public rates track older gear.

falsifiableTrigger: exportControlExposure eases so China DC revenue recovers above prior levels within 2 quarters.
mechanism: Licence rules and tariffs put a large block of Chinese buyers out of reach, so vendors cannot sell into demand that plainly exists.
rationale: NVIDIA recorded no data-center Hopper shipments to China against $4.6 billion a year earlier, China revenue fell to $4,550 million from $9,659 million, and NVIDIA assumes no China data-center compute revenue in its outlook. It also more than halved the number of authorised Asian buyers under a new compliance whitelist, H200 shipments remain trivial despite about $10 billion of approved licences, and AMD took roughly $440 million of charges with a 25% tariff and US inspection on any MI325 sent to China.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether approved licences turn into actual shipments; so far the paperwork exists and the volume does not.

falsifiableTrigger: Vendor-financed GPU commitments in rpoBacklog exceed 300,000 units within 2 quarters.
mechanism: The chip seller lends or guarantees the money its customers use to buy chips, so reported demand partly reflects the seller's own credit rather than independent buying power.
rationale: NVIDIA is discussing a $350 billion facility for OpenAI chip purchases and up to $250 billion of backstop for OpenAI compute leases, and has scaled a chief-financial-officer-approved programme that guarantees purchases, rents back idle capacity and takes revenue share, covering about 210,000 GPUs at Firmus and Sharon AI after $6.3 billion for CoreWeave and $1.5 billion for Lambda. It raised $25 billion in bonds in June to fund the programme, invested in Safe Superintelligence alongside a compute commitment, and AMD committed up to $5 billion of equity in Anthropic alongside its own deal.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the financed buyers can service their own debt without the guarantees; a single default would expose the loop.

falsifiableTrigger: customerConcentration for the top three direct customers falls below prior shares next fiscal year.
mechanism: A handful of buyers place most of the orders, so one of them slowing down or switching to its own chips removes a large slice of revenue at once.
rationale: NVIDIA disclosed three direct customers at 21%, 17% and 16% of total revenue, and in the prior fiscal year one customer at 22% and another at 14%, up from 12%, 11% and 11%, with the four largest now more than half of revenue. SpaceX adds a new concentrated claim, saying its understanding is that it will receive a very significant percentage of NVIDIA's 2027 output and that it will build exclusively on NVIDIA.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether new buyer tiers such as national projects and enterprises grow fast enough to dilute the top handful.

falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA DC Ethernet switch market-share-pct slips from #1 within 2 quarters.
mechanism: Selling the switches and optics with the accelerators makes the whole cluster one purchase, so swapping in another vendor's chip means rebuilding the network too.
rationale: NVIDIA became the revenue leader in data-center Ethernet switching for the first time in the first quarter of 2026, tied to networking bundled with its accelerator deployments. Its newest switch generation named CoreWeave, Microsoft, Nebius, SpaceXAI and Tesla as first customers, its photonics claims 5x better power efficiency and up to 95% network efficiency across deployments above 100,000 GPUs, and it signed a long-term deal with Corning to expand US optical capacity tenfold.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to open rack standards; AMD is co-developing rack-scale standards with Meta that would let buyers mix parts.

falsifiableTrigger: Cost-per-token gains stall so tokenEconomics improves less than one generation cycle.
mechanism: When each new generation cuts the price of serving a token, work that was too expensive to run becomes worth running, so total accelerator hours grow.
rationale: The newest NVIDIA generation on Google Cloud is claimed to deliver 10x lower inference cost per token than the prior generation and one-tenth the cost per million tokens versus the previous flagship rack, extending an order-of-magnitude cost drop already claimed for the current generation. Open-source inference costs have fallen 30 to 50 percent a year since 2023, AT&T is described as burning about 1 trillion tokens a month, and SpaceX expects roughly 90% of its compute to serve inference or be rented out.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether rivals match the cost-per-token drop; AMD claims 30% more tokens per dollar on its own rack.

falsifiableTrigger: Prepaid HBM commitments in rpoBacklog shrink or deposits are refunded within a quarter.
mechanism: Buyers who put cash down years ahead for memory cannot walk away without losing it, so their future accelerator purchases are effectively already committed.
rationale: Micron's 16 non-cancelable five-year take-or-pay agreements backed by more than $22 billion of cash and commitments, including nearly $18 billion of deposits, still stand as the anchor evidence. Suppliers sold out their entire 2026 production under non-cancellable contracts at high-teen to low-twenties percent price increases, with order books extending into 2028, but no new prepaid contract was reported this cycle.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether memory suppliers keep signing new prepaid deals; without fresh contracts the lock-in ages out.

falsifiableTrigger: exportControlExposure changes lift the sub-50% China cap or clear Blackwell within 2 quarters.
mechanism: Case-by-case licences with a hard percentage cap let a trickle of older parts through while keeping the newest ones out, so the opening exists on paper more than in volume.
rationale: The January 15 rule shifting H200-class chips from presumption of denial to case-by-case review still stands, with a 25% tariff and a cap of under 50% of same-model US sales. Shipments have begun to about ten approved buyers including Tencent, ByteDance and Alibaba, but volumes remain trivial against roughly $10 billion of approved licences, each firm capped at 75,000 chips, and Chinese orders of over two million parts against roughly 700,000 units of inventory.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to the tariff and security conditions attached to each licence, which have so far kept approved orders from turning into shipments.

falsifiableTrigger: Memory hbmSupplyCapex expansion pulls DRAM/NVMe prices down within 2 quarters.
mechanism: Memory and storage are a large slice of the bill of materials, so when their prices jump the cost of every rack rises and the builder absorbs or passes on the difference.
rationale: Rack component costs are running up about 2 to 3 percent a week and sit 10 to 15 percent above baseline on memory and storage scarcity, memory component lead times have stretched to 32 to 40-plus weeks with prices up about 90% since late 2025, and server memory contract prices are expected to rise more than 25% quarter over quarter. Samsung is seeking up to a 20% price increase with quote validity cut to 72 hours, and AMD reports its accelerator revenue carries a gross margin slightly below its corporate average.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to when new memory fabs come online; capacity announced today does not ship parts until late 2026 at the earliest.

falsifiableTrigger: releaseCadence slips push a major vendor's 2H-2026 ramp into 2027.
mechanism: Each vendor hits volume production on its own schedule, so new supply arrives in waves over several quarters rather than all at once.
rationale: The staged picture holds. NVIDIA's newest rack entered production ramp with deployments at CoreWeave, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure and Oracle, AMD's rack reached full production with shipments starting in the third quarter of 2026 and the ramp running into the second half of 2027, one account still puts AMD's first production output at the second quarter of 2027, Meta's in-house parts enter production in September, and supply-chain reporting has all the next-generation parts moving into mass production together.
sensitivity: Most sensitive to manufacturing delays at AMD, where accounts differ on whether real volume lands in late 2026 or mid-2027.

falsifiableTrigger: AMD customerConcentration eases as its buyer base broadens over the next 2 quarters.
mechanism: A few very large commitments carry most of AMD's accelerator growth, so one partner delaying or cancelling swings the whole line.
